records.greek: Μετὰ ταῦτα ἀπῆλθεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς πέραν τῆς θαλάσσης τῆς Γαλιλαίας τῆς Τιβεριάδος.
records.gloss: After these things went away the Jesus across the sea of the Galilee of the Tiberias.
pieces: , which is also called the Sea

L.1: After these things Jesus went off across the Sea of Galilee, [the Sea] of Tiberias.

R.1: After this, Jesus went across to the other side of the Sea of Galilee. This large lake was also called the Sea of Tiberias.

decisions.choice: of Tiberias: a second name for the same lake
decisions.reason: Herod Antipas founded the city of Tiberias on the western shore of the lake in about AD 20 and named it after the emperor Tiberius. In time the lake itself came to be called after the city, and John gives both names, perhaps for readers who knew it by the newer one. He uses the newer name alone in 21:1.

decisions.choice: after these things: a loose link of time, with no length given
alternatives: immediately after the events of chapter 5
decisions.reason: John often moves on to a new episode with this phrase (3:22; 5:1; 7:1). Chapter 5 took place in Jerusalem and this one in Galilee, and John does not say how much time passed between them or how Jesus came back north.

decisions.choice: across the sea: to the other shore of the Lake of Galilee
decisions.reason: The word means "sea", but here it is the freshwater lake of Galilee, about 13 miles (21 km) long. John does not say which shore Jesus reached. The boats from Tiberias in verse 23 and the return to Capernaum in verses 17 and 24 suggest a quieter place away from the towns of the western and northern shores; Luke 9:10 places the feeding near Bethsaida.

decisions.choice: [the Sea] of Tiberias (L); which is also called the Sea of Tiberias (B); This large lake was also called (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek simply adds the second name. Literal brackets the words needed to make it read as a name of the same lake; Balanced and Readable say plainly that it is a second name (meaning decision m1), and Readable says that this "sea" is a lake.

records.heading: Jesus feeds five thousand

records.greek: ἠκολούθει δὲ αὐτῷ ὄχλος πολύς, ὅτι ἐθεώρουν τὰ σημεῖα ἃ ἐποίει ἐπὶ τῶν ἀσθενούντων.
records.gloss: Was following now him a crowd large, because they were seeing the signs which he was doing on the [ones] being sick.

L.2: Now a great crowd was following Him, because they were watching the signs which He was doing upon those who were sick.

R.2: A huge crowd of people kept following Him. They had seen the signs He was doing when He healed sick people.

decisions.choice: was following, were seeing, was doing: ongoing action
decisions.reason: All three verbs describe something that went on over a period: the crowd kept following him, because they kept seeing the signs he kept doing.

decisions.choice: signs: deeds of power that point to who Jesus is; here, healings of the sick
decisions.reason: John calls Jesus's deeds "signs" because they point beyond themselves (2:11; 20:30-31). The ones meant here are healings, done "on" the sick, such as those at 4:46-54 and 5:1-9.

decisions.choice: the crowd follows because of the signs, not yet because it understands them
decisions.reason: John often shows people drawn by the signs without grasping what they point to (2:23-25). Jesus says this of this very crowd the next day: they looked for him because they ate the bread, not because they saw signs (6:26).

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}
decisions.reason: Every pronoun for Christ uses the deity_pronoun setting, including "you" when people speak to him. At the start of a sentence "He" is written plain. This applies throughout the passage.

decisions.choice: by healing the sick (B); when he healed sick people (R)
decisions.reason: "Doing signs on the sick" means healing them (meaning decision m2); Balanced and Readable say so.

records.greek: ἀνῆλθεν δὲ εἰς τὸ ὄρος Ἰησοῦς, καὶ ἐκεῖ ἐκάθητο μετὰ τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: Went up now into the mountain Jesus, and there was sitting with the disciples of him.

L.3: And Jesus went up onto the mountain, and there He was sitting with His disciples.

R.3: Jesus went up into the hills and sat down there with His disciples.

decisions.choice: the mountain: the hill country rising from the shore of the lake
decisions.reason: The word can mean a mountain or the hills in general. The article probably points to the hills by the lake rather than a named peak; no mountain is named, and the crowd can reach the place on foot (verse 5).

decisions.choice: going up the mountain: a possible echo of Moses
decisions.reason: The chapter is set near Passover (verse 4) and soon compares Jesus with Moses and the manna (6:14, 31-32). Moses went up the mountain to meet God (Exodus 19:3; 24:12-18), and some readers hear an echo. The words are also an ordinary description of the scene, so the echo is possible but not certain.

decisions.choice: sitting: the posture of a teacher with his disciples
decisions.reason: Teachers in Israel sat to teach (Matthew 5:1; Luke 4:20). The imperfect tense pictures Jesus settled there with the disciples when the crowd arrives.

decisions.choice: the hills
decisions.reason: "The mountain" suggests one peak; Balanced and Readable say "hills" for the hill country by the lake (meaning decision m1). Verse 15 uses the same word the same way.

records.greek: ἦν δὲ ἐγγὺς τὸ πάσχα, ἡ ἑορτὴ τῶν Ἰουδαίων.
records.gloss: Was now near the Passover, the feast of the Jews.

L.4: Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was near.

R.4: It was almost time for Passover. This was the Jewish festival when people remembered how God had set Israel free from Egypt.

decisions.choice: Passover: the spring festival that remembered the exodus from Egypt
decisions.reason: Passover was kept in the spring, in the month of Nisan (Exodus 12). It is the second of three Passovers John mentions (2:13; 11:55), and it explains why there was plenty of green grass in verse 10. Jesus is not said to go up to Jerusalem for it.

decisions.choice: the note about Passover sets the feeding and the teaching that follows in the light of the exodus
decisions.reason: What follows recalls Israel's escape from Egypt: bread given in a lonely place, a prophet like Moses (verse 14), a crossing of the sea (verses 16-21), and the talk of manna and the true bread from heaven (6:31-35). At the final Passover Jesus dies as the Lamb of God (1:29; 19:14, 36). John mentions the festival here to point the reader that way.

decisions.choice: the Jews: the Jewish people, whose festival it was
decisions.reason: As at 2:13 and 5:1, John names the festival as the people's, for readers who did not keep it.

decisions.choice: the Jewish festival
decisions.reason: Here the word means the Jewish people (meaning decision m3), so Balanced and Readable say "Jewish" without naming the leaders.

decisions.choice: when people remembered how God had set Israel free from Egypt
decisions.reason: Readable explains what Passover was, since the passage depends on it (meaning decisions m1 and m2).

records.greek: ἐπάρας οὖν τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς ὁ Ἰησοῦς καὶ θεασάμενος ὅτι πολὺς ὄχλος ἔρχεται πρὸς αὐτὸν λέγει πρὸς Φίλιππον· Πόθεν ἀγοράσωμεν ἄρτους ἵνα φάγωσιν οὗτοι;
records.gloss: Having lifted up then the eyes the Jesus and having seen that a large crowd is coming toward him, says to Philip, "From where may we buy loaves so that may eat these?"

L.5: So Jesus, lifting up His eyes and seeing that a great crowd is coming toward Him, says to Philip, "From where are we to buy loaves, so that these [people] may eat?"

R.5: Jesus looked up and saw a big crowd coming to Him. He asked Philip, "Where can we buy bread so that all these people can eat?"

decisions.choice: lifting up his eyes: looking up and taking notice
decisions.reason: The phrase is a Hebrew way of saying that someone looked up attentively at what was before him (Genesis 18:2; John 4:35; 17:1).

decisions.choice: from where are we to buy bread: a question that recalls Moses in the wilderness
decisions.reason: "From where" asks about the source, not just the shop. In the wilderness Moses asked God, "Where am I to get meat to give to all this people?" (Numbers 11:13). In this Passover setting (verse 4) the question echoes his; the answer is that the bread will come from Jesus himself. By saying "we", Jesus draws the disciples into the problem.

decisions.choice: Philip: a disciple from Bethsaida, near the place
decisions.reason: Philip came from Bethsaida (1:44), a town at the north end of the lake, so he was a natural person to ask about where food could be found nearby.

decisions.choice: asked
decisions.reason: John often tells a story in the present tense ("he says", "they see") for vividness. Literal keeps the present; Balanced and Readable use the past, as stories are normally told in this language. This applies to every such verb in the passage (verses 5, 8, 12, 19 and 20).

decisions.choice: bread
decisions.reason: The word means loaves: flat, round breads that were the basic food of every meal. Balanced and Readable say "bread" here; verse 9 counts them as loaves.

records.greek: τοῦτο δὲ ἔλεγεν πειράζων αὐτόν, αὐτὸς γὰρ ᾔδει τί ἔμελλεν ποιεῖν.
records.gloss: This now he was saying testing him, he himself for knew what he was about to do.

L.6: Now He was saying this to test him, for He Himself knew what He was about to do.

R.6: Jesus asked this to test Philip. Jesus already knew what He was going to do.

decisions.choice: testing: drawing out Philip's understanding and trust
decisions.reason: The verb can mean either to test or to tempt. Here Jesus does not lead Philip into wrong; he gives him the chance to show whether he will look to Jesus for what is needed. In the exodus story God "tested" Israel with the manna (Exodus 16:4).

decisions.choice: for he himself knew: a comment by the narrator
decisions.reason: John steps in to explain that the question was not because Jesus did not know what to do. He often notes what Jesus knew beforehand (2:24-25; 6:64; 13:1-3).

decisions.choice: Jesus ... Philip
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name both men, since "he" and "him" refer to different people in this short sentence.

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθη αὐτῷ Φίλιππος· Διακοσίων δηναρίων ἄρτοι οὐκ ἀρκοῦσιν αὐτοῖς ἵνα ἕκαστος βραχύ τι λάβῃ.
records.gloss: Answered him Philip, "Of two hundred denarii loaves not are enough for them, so that each a little something may receive."
pieces: costing more than half a year's wages

L.7: Philip answered Him, "Two hundred denarii [worth] of loaves are not enough for them, for each to receive a little something."

R.7: Philip answered, "Even if we spent more than half a year's pay on bread, there would not be enough for each person to have a small piece."

decisions.choice: two hundred denarii: about two hundred days' wages
decisions.reason: A denarius was a silver coin, the usual pay for a laborer's day of work (Matthew 20:2). Two hundred denarii was the pay for more than half a year of working days, far more than a group of traveling disciples would carry.

decisions.choice: are not enough: Philip counts the cost and finds the task impossible
decisions.reason: Jesus asked where bread could come from; Philip answers with what it would cost, and even that sum would give each person only a taste. The answer shows that he is looking for a way that does not depend on Jesus (verse 6).

decisions.choice: {{units:more than half a year's wages|two hundred denarii}} (B); {{units:more than half a year's pay|two hundred denarii}} (R)
decisions.reason: The coin means nothing to most readers, so Balanced and Readable give its value in wages by default, and the units setting shows the original "two hundred denarii". Literal always keeps the coin.

decisions.choice: Two hundred denarii [worth] of loaves
decisions.reason: The Greek says "loaves of two hundred denarii", meaning loaves costing that much; Literal brackets the word needed to say so.

records.greek: λέγει αὐτῷ εἷς ἐκ τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτοῦ, Ἀνδρέας ὁ ἀδελφὸς Σίμωνος Πέτρου·
records.gloss: Says to him one of the disciples of him, Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter,

L.8: One of His disciples, Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, says to Him,

R.8: Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, was another of the disciples. He said to Jesus,

decisions.choice: Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter: one of the first disciples, from the same town as Philip
decisions.reason: Andrew was among the first to follow Jesus, and he brought his brother Simon to him (1:40-42). He and Philip both came from Bethsaida (1:44), and they appear together again at 12:22. Here once more Andrew brings someone to Jesus.

decisions.choice: one of his disciples: a second disciple, besides Philip, speaks
decisions.reason: Jesus put the question to Philip, but Andrew joins in with what he has found; the speech itself follows in the next sentence.

decisions.choice: He said to Jesus
decisions.reason: Readable breaks the introduction into two short sentences and names Jesus as the one Andrew speaks to.

records.greek: Ἔστιν παιδάριον ὧδε ὃς ἔχει πέντε ἄρτους κριθίνους καὶ δύο ὀψάρια· ἀλλὰ ταῦτα τί ἐστιν εἰς τοσούτους;
records.gloss: "There is a little boy here who has five loaves barley and two fish; but these what are for so many?"

L.9: "A little boy is here who has five loaves of barley and two small fish; but these, what are [they] for so many?"

R.9: "A boy here has five small loaves of barley bread and two little fish. But that will not help much with so many people!"

decisions.choice: a little boy: a child or a young lad
decisions.reason: The word is a diminutive of the word for a child, and can also mean a young servant. Nothing here says he was a servant; he is simply a boy in the crowd who has some food with him. His exact age is not given.

decisions.choice: barley loaves: the cheap bread of poor people
decisions.reason: Barley was cheaper than wheat and was the usual bread of the poor (compare Revelation 6:6, where barley costs a third the price of wheat). Only John says the loaves were barley.

decisions.choice: barley loaves for a crowd: an echo of Elisha
decisions.reason: In 2 Kings 4:42-44 a man brings the prophet Elisha twenty barley loaves; his servant asks how that can feed a hundred men, and the men eat and have some left over, as the LORD had said. Here barley loaves, the question "what are these for so many?" and the leftovers (verses 12-13) follow the same pattern, on a far greater scale.

decisions.choice: fish: small fish, eaten with bread
decisions.reason: The word is a diminutive and was used of fish prepared to eat with bread, often dried or salted. Fish from the lake were salted and traded around Galilee.

decisions.choice: small fish (L, B); little fish (R)
decisions.reason: Every level shows that these were small fish (meaning decision m4).

decisions.choice: what good is that with so many people? (B); that will not help much with so many people! (R)
alternatives: what are these for so many? (Literal)
decisions.reason: Andrew's question expects the answer "nothing"; Balanced asks it in everyday words and Readable states what it means.

records.greek: εἶπεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ποιήσατε τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἀναπεσεῖν.
records.gloss: Said the Jesus, "Make the people to recline."

R.10: Jesus said, "Tell everyone to sit down."

decisions.choice: recline: settle on the ground for a meal
decisions.reason: At a meal people reclined, leaning on one elbow (13:23). On a hillside this meant sitting or lying on the grass. The word tells the crowd that they are about to be fed.

decisions.choice: the people: the whole crowd, men and women
decisions.reason: This word means human beings in general. When John counts them in the next sentence, he uses a different word that means men specifically.

decisions.choice: {{gender:people|men}}
decisions.reason: The word is inclusive (meaning decision m2), so the default is "people"; the gender setting gives the traditional "men". Readable says "everyone", which needs no setting.

decisions.choice: sit down
decisions.reason: "Recline" sounds like a couch; on a grassy hillside "sit down" says what the people did.

records.greek: ἦν δὲ χόρτος πολὺς ἐν τῷ τόπῳ.
records.gloss: Was now grass much in the place.

L.10: Now much grass was in that place.

R.10: The ground there was covered with grass.

decisions.choice: much grass: the hills were green in spring
decisions.reason: Passover was near (verse 4), at the end of the rainy season, when the hills of Galilee are green; later in the year the grass is dry and brown. The detail fits the season John has named.

decisions.choice: much grass: possibly an echo of the shepherd who makes his flock lie down in green pastures
alternatives: a detail of the scene only
decisions.reason: Psalm 23:2 pictures the LORD as a shepherd who makes his sheep lie down in green pastures, and Jesus will call himself the good shepherd (10:11). Some readers see that picture here, as the people lie down and are fed. John does not point it out.

records.greek: ἀνέπεσαν οὖν οἱ ἄνδρες τὸν ἀριθμὸν ὡς πεντακισχίλιοι.
records.gloss: Reclined then the men the number about five thousand.

L.10: So the men reclined, in number about 5,000.

R.10: So the men sat down. There were about 5,000 of them.

decisions.choice: the men: adult males, the ones who were counted
alternatives: the whole crowd, men and women together
decisions.reason: John changes from the general word for people (the first sentence of this verse) to the word for men. It was usual to count the men of a gathering (Exodus 12:37; Numbers 1:2-3). Matthew 14:21 says that women and children were there besides; John gives only the number of men.

decisions.choice: about five thousand: a round figure
decisions.reason: "About" shows that this is an estimate, not an exact count.
Numbers above ninety-nine are written in numerals at every level.

decisions.choice: sat down
decisions.reason: As in the first sentence of this verse.

records.greek: ἔλαβεν οὖν τοὺς ἄρτους ὁ Ἰησοῦς καὶ εὐχαριστήσας διέδωκεν τοῖς ἀνακειμένοις, ὁμοίως καὶ ἐκ τῶν ὀψαρίων ὅσον ἤθελον.
records.gloss: Took then the loaves the Jesus and having given thanks distributed to the [ones] reclining, likewise also from the fish as much as they were wanting.

L.11: So Jesus took the loaves, and after giving thanks He handed [them] out to those reclining; in the same way also from the fish, as much as they were wanting.

R.11: Jesus took the loaves and thanked God for them. Then He gave the bread to the people who were sitting there. He gave out the fish in the same way. Everyone had as much as they wanted.

decisions.choice: having given thanks: the blessing said over bread before a meal
decisions.reason: Before a meal the head of the household took the bread and gave thanks to God for it. Jesus does what any Jewish host would do, and John recalls it again in 6:23: "where they ate the bread after the Lord had given thanks".

decisions.choice: gave thanks: an ordinary meal blessing, with a possible echo of the Lord's Supper
alternatives: a deliberate picture of the Lord's Supper
decisions.reason: This verb, which gave the Lord's Supper its later name, the Eucharist, is used when Jesus gives thanks over the bread at the Last Supper (Luke 22:19; 1 Corinthians 11:24). John tells no such scene at the supper, and later in this chapter Jesus speaks of eating his flesh and drinking his blood (6:51-58). Readers who knew the church's meal could hear an echo in "took the loaves, gave thanks, and distributed". But the words are also the normal way to describe a Jewish meal, and the text does not make the link itself.

decisions.choice: he distributed to those reclining (SBLGNT): Jesus himself hands out the food
alternatives: he distributed to the disciples, and the disciples to those reclining (later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add that Jesus gave the bread to the disciples and they gave it to the people, as Matthew 14:19, Mark 6:41 and Luke 9:16 say. The earliest manuscripts do not have these words, and they look like an addition to bring John into line with the other Gospels. In John's text the gift comes straight from Jesus's hands. A footnote gives the longer reading. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: as much as they wanted: there was no rationing
decisions.reason: Philip expected each to get only a little (verse 7); instead each one had as much as he wanted, and there was more left over (verses 12-13).

decisions.choice: thanked God for them
decisions.reason: Readable says to whom the thanks were given, which the Greek takes for granted (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: shared them out (B); gave (R)
decisions.reason: Everyday words for giving each person a share.

records.greek: ὡς δὲ ἐνεπλήσθησαν λέγει τοῖς μαθηταῖς αὐτοῦ· Συναγάγετε τὰ περισσεύσαντα κλάσματα, ἵνα μή τι ἀπόληται.
records.gloss: When now they were filled, he says to the disciples of him, "Gather the having been left over fragments, so that not anything may be lost."

L.12: And when they were filled, He says to His disciples, "Gather the broken pieces that are left over, so that not anything may be lost."

R.12: When everyone was full, Jesus told His disciples, "Pick up all the pieces of food that are left. Do not let any of it be lost."

decisions.choice: they were filled: they had eaten until they were satisfied
decisions.reason: The verb means to be filled full. The point is plenty, set against Philip's "each a little" (verse 7).

decisions.choice: fragments: pieces broken off the loaves
decisions.reason: The word means broken pieces. These are the pieces broken off for the people and not eaten, not scraps they had dropped.

decisions.choice: so that nothing may be lost: not to waste the food, with an echo of Jesus losing none of those given to him
alternatives: only a matter of not wasting food
decisions.reason: The plain sense is not to waste good food. But the same verb is used in this chapter for what Jesus will not let happen to those the Father gives him: "that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me" (6:39; also 3:16; 17:12; 18:9). John may want the reader to hear that echo. In the exodus story the manna could not be kept and spoiled (Exodus 16:19-20); this bread is gathered up.

decisions.choice: told
decisions.reason: The historic present; see the note at verse 5.

decisions.choice: be lost (L, R); is lost (B)
decisions.reason: Every level keeps "lost", so that the echo of 6:39 noted in meaning decision m3 stays visible.

records.greek: συνήγαγον οὖν, καὶ ἐγέμισαν δώδεκα κοφίνους κλασμάτων ἐκ τῶν πέντε ἄρτων τῶν κριθίνων ἃ ἐπερίσσευσαν τοῖς βεβρωκόσιν.
records.gloss: They gathered then, and filled twelve baskets of fragments from the five loaves the barley which were left over to the [ones] having eaten.

L.13: So they gathered [them] and filled twelve baskets of pieces from the five loaves of barley, which were more than those who had eaten [needed].

R.13: So the disciples gathered the pieces. They filled twelve baskets with what was left from the five barley loaves after everyone had eaten.

decisions.choice: baskets: good-sized baskets of the kind travelers carried
decisions.reason: This is the word for a stout wicker basket used for carrying food and goods. Twelve full baskets is far more than the five loaves the meal began with.

decisions.choice: twelve: possibly pointing to the twelve tribes of Israel and the twelve disciples
alternatives: a count with no further meaning
decisions.reason: There may simply have been one basket for each of the twelve disciples (6:67-70). The number twelve also stands for the people of Israel, and some readers see a sign that Jesus provides for all God's people. John does not draw that out.

decisions.choice: which were left over to those who had eaten: the surplus beyond what the people ate
decisions.reason: The pieces were more than the people needed, as in Elisha's feeding, where "they ate and had some left" (2 Kings 4:44).

decisions.choice: gathered [them]; more than ... [needed]
decisions.reason: Literal brackets the words English needs to complete the two phrases.

decisions.choice: the disciples
decisions.reason: Readable names who did the gathering (verse 12).

records.greek: οἱ οὖν ἄνθρωποι ἰδόντες ὃ ἐποίησεν σημεῖον ἔλεγον ὅτι Οὗτός ἐστιν ἀληθῶς ὁ προφήτης ὁ ἐρχόμενος εἰς τὸν κόσμον.
records.gloss: The then people having seen what he did sign were saying, "This is truly the prophet the [one] coming into the world."

L.14: So the people, having seen the sign that He did, were saying, "This is truly the Prophet who is coming into the world."

R.14: The people saw this sign that Jesus had done. They said, "This man really must be the Prophet whom God promised to send into the world!"

decisions.choice: the sign that he did, singular (SBLGNT)
alternatives: the signs that he did, plural (some manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts have the plural, "signs", perhaps under the influence of verse 2. The singular, pointing to the feeding just done, is the better-supported reading. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the Prophet: the prophet like Moses whom God promised to raise up
alternatives: a prophet in a general sense
decisions.reason: In Deuteronomy 18:15-18 Moses tells Israel that God will raise up a prophet like him. In John's day people looked for this Prophet (1:21, 25; 7:40). After bread given in a lonely place, as Moses' people received manna, the crowd draws the comparison. The comparison is right as far as it goes, but Jesus will say that it was not Moses who gave the bread from heaven (6:32).

decisions.choice: coming into the world: the expected one who comes from God to humanity; world means the world of people
decisions.reason: "The one coming" was a way of speaking of the one God would send (11:27; Matthew 11:3). "The world" here is the world of human beings, to whom he comes, as at 1:9 and 3:19.

decisions.choice: were saying: the imperfect shows the talk spreading through the crowd
decisions.reason: The tense pictures people saying it to one another, which leads to the plan in verse 15.

decisions.choice: the Prophet, with a capital
decisions.reason: A capital shows that the crowd means one particular expected figure (meaning decision m2), not any prophet.

decisions.choice: whom God promised to send
decisions.reason: Readable explains which prophet is meant (Deuteronomy 18:15-18). The crowd knew the promise, so this does not put anything in their mouths that they did not know.

decisions.choice: {{gender:people|men}}
decisions.reason: The general word for people, as in verse 10; the gender setting gives the traditional "men".

records.greek: Ἰησοῦς οὖν γνοὺς ὅτι μέλλουσιν ἔρχεσθαι καὶ ἁρπάζειν αὐτὸν ἵνα ποιήσωσιν βασιλέα ἀνεχώρησεν πάλιν εἰς τὸ ὄρος αὐτὸς μόνος.
records.gloss: Jesus then having known that they are about to come and to seize him so that they may make [him] king, withdrew again into the mountain he himself alone.

L.15: So Jesus, knowing that they were about to come and seize Him in order to make [Him] king, withdrew again to the mountain, alone by Himself.

R.15: Jesus knew that the people were planning to grab Him and force Him to be their king. So He slipped away again, up into the hills, all by Himself.

decisions.choice: seize: take by force
decisions.reason: The verb means to snatch or carry off by force. The crowd means to make him king whether he wishes it or not.

decisions.choice: make him king: the hope for a leader who would free Israel from Rome
decisions.reason: Many in Galilee hoped for a king like David who would drive out the Romans; a prophet like Moses who fed the people seemed just such a leader. Jesus refuses this kind of kingship. He is a king, but his kingdom is not from this world (18:36-37).

decisions.choice: knowing: Jesus knew their plan before they acted
decisions.reason: John does not say how Jesus knew; he often notes that Jesus knew what was in people (2:24-25).

decisions.choice: again to the mountain: back to the hills of verse 3
decisions.reason: "Again" looks back to verse 3. Jesus had been in the hills with his disciples; now he goes back up alone, leaving the disciples behind (verse 16).

decisions.choice: the hills
decisions.reason: As in verse 3.

records.greek: Ὡς δὲ ὀψία ἐγένετο κατέβησαν οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ τὴν θάλασσαν, καὶ ἐμβάντες εἰς πλοῖον ἤρχοντο πέραν τῆς θαλάσσης εἰς Καφαρναούμ.
records.gloss: When now evening came went down the disciples of him to the sea, \v 17 and having embarked into a boat they were going across the sea to Capernaum.

L.16: Now as evening came on, His disciples went down to the sea,
L.17: and having stepped into a boat, they were heading across the sea to Capernaum.

R.16: That evening, Jesus's disciples went down to the lake.
R.17: They got into a boat and started across the lake to the town of Capernaum.

decisions.choice: Capernaum: a town on the northwest shore, where Jesus often stayed
decisions.reason: Capernaum was a fishing town on the northern shore of the lake (2:12). The crowd looks for Jesus there the next day (6:24), and he teaches there in the synagogue (6:59).

decisions.choice: they were going: the crossing had begun but was not finished
decisions.reason: The imperfect describes a journey under way. It sets the scene for what happens on the water.

decisions.choice: evening: late in the day, toward dusk
decisions.reason: The word covers late afternoon and the beginning of night. By the next sentence it is fully dark.

decisions.choice: the lake
decisions.reason: The Greek word is "sea". Literal and Balanced keep it, so the thread of the sea through the passage stays visible; Readable says "lake", which is what it was (see verse 1).

decisions.choice: Jesus's disciples; the town of
decisions.reason: Readable names Jesus, who has been off alone since the last sentence, and says that Capernaum was a town.

records.heading: Jesus walks on the sea

records.greek: καὶ σκοτία ἤδη ἐγεγόνει καὶ οὔπω ἐληλύθει πρὸς αὐτοὺς ὁ Ἰησοῦς, ἥ τε θάλασσα ἀνέμου μεγάλου πνέοντος διεγείρετο.
records.gloss: And darkness already had come and not yet had come to them the Jesus, \v 18 the and sea, a wind great blowing, was being stirred up.

L.17: And darkness had already come, and Jesus had not yet come to them;
L.18: and the sea was being stirred up, a great wind blowing.

R.17: It was already dark, and Jesus had not come to them yet.
R.18: A strong wind was blowing, and the lake was getting very rough.

decisions.choice: had not yet come to them: the disciples were without Jesus, and the reader is told he will come
alternatives: they had arranged to pick him up on the way
decisions.reason: "Not yet" suggests that his coming was expected, at least by the narrator. John does not say whether the disciples had agreed to meet him; the words prepare for verse 19.

decisions.choice: darkness: night had fallen, with a possible hint of John's theme of darkness
decisions.reason: John uses this word for the darkness that cannot overcome the light (1:5; 8:12; 12:35, 46). Here it means plainly that night had come; the disciples in the dark without Jesus may also be a picture of that theme, but this is not stated.

decisions.choice: was being stirred up: the waves were growing because a strong wind was blowing
decisions.reason: The imperfect pictures the sea becoming rougher; the participle about the wind gives the cause. Sudden strong winds come down on the lake from the hills around it.

decisions.choice: The sea was getting rough, whipped up by a strong wind (B); A strong wind was blowing, and the lake was getting very rough (R)
alternatives: the sea was being stirred up, a great wind blowing (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make the wind the plain cause of the rough water, as the Greek participle implies.

records.greek: ἐληλακότες οὖν ὡς σταδίους εἴκοσι πέντε ἢ τριάκοντα θεωροῦσιν τὸν Ἰησοῦν περιπατοῦντα ἐπὶ τῆς θαλάσσης καὶ ἐγγὺς τοῦ πλοίου γινόμενον, καὶ ἐφοβήθησαν.
records.gloss: Having rowed then about stadia twenty-five or thirty they see the Jesus walking on the sea and near the boat coming, and they were afraid.

L.19: So when they had rowed about twenty-five or thirty stadia, they see Jesus walking on the sea and drawing near to the boat, and they became afraid.

R.19: They had rowed about 3 or 3½ miles when they saw Jesus walking on top of the water toward the boat. They were frightened.

decisions.choice: twenty-five or thirty stadia: about three to three and a half miles
decisions.reason: A stadion was about 600 feet (185 meters), so twenty-five or thirty of them come to about 4.5 to 5.5 kilometers. The lake is about seven miles across at its widest, so the disciples were far out on the water.

decisions.choice: walking on the sea: on the surface of the water
alternatives: walking by the sea, along the shore
decisions.reason: The same words can mean "by the sea" (21:1), and that has been suggested here. But the disciples are miles out, they are afraid, and Jesus comes near the boat; John tells a wonder, as Matthew 14:25 and Mark 6:48 also do.

decisions.choice: walking on the sea: an act the Scriptures give to God alone
decisions.reason: In the Scriptures God is the one who "treads on the waves of the sea" (Job 9:8) and whose "path was through the sea" (Psalm 77:20, at the exodus). With the Passover setting (verse 4) and Jesus's words in verse 20, the scene points to who Jesus is.

decisions.choice: they were afraid: fear at what they saw, not only at the storm
decisions.reason: John does not mention fear of the waves; the disciples are afraid when they see Jesus on the water (compare Mark 6:49-50).

decisions.choice: about {{units:3 or 3½ miles|twenty-five or thirty stadia}}
decisions.reason: The stadion means nothing to most readers, so Balanced and Readable give the distance in miles by default, and the units setting shows the original measure. Numerals are used in measurements. Literal always keeps the ancient unit.

decisions.choice: caught sight of (B); saw (R)
decisions.reason: The historic present; see the note at verse 5.

records.greek: ὁ δὲ λέγει αὐτοῖς· Ἐγώ εἰμι, μὴ φοβεῖσθε.
records.gloss: He but says to them, "I am; not be afraid."

L.20: But He says to them, "I am [He]; do not be afraid."

R.20: But He said to them, "It is me! Do not be afraid."

decisions.choice: I am: plainly "it is I", with an echo of the way God names himself
alternatives: the divine name, I AM, as the main sense
only the plain sense, with no echo
decisions.reason: The words have no predicate. To frightened men in a boat at night the plain sense is "it is I", the one you know. But these are also the words with which God speaks of himself in the Greek of Isaiah: "I am" (Isaiah 43:10; 51:12), and in the same chapter, "Do not fear ... when you pass through the waters, I will be with you" (Isaiah 43:1-2). Jesus says them while doing what Scripture gives to God alone (verse 19, meaning decision m3 there). The plain sense is uppermost, and the echo is likely; later in John the bare "I am" carries it more clearly (8:24, 28, 58). Marked uncertain; a footnote gives the bare "I am".

decisions.choice: do not be afraid: stop being afraid
decisions.reason: The present tense with "not" tells them to stop the fear they already have (verse 19). In the Scriptures God and his messengers often say these words when they appear (Genesis 15:1; Isaiah 43:1; Luke 1:30).

decisions.choice: I am [he] (L); It is I (B); It is me (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek has only "I am". Literal brackets the "he" that the plain sense needs, and it takes the deity_pronoun setting as a pronoun for Christ; Balanced and Readable say the plain sense in everyday words. The footnote gives the bare words, so the echo noted in meaning decision m1 stays visible.

decisions.choice: told (B); said (R)
decisions.reason: The historic present; see the note at verse 5.

records.greek: ἤθελον οὖν λαβεῖν αὐτὸν εἰς τὸ πλοῖον, καὶ εὐθέως ἐγένετο τὸ πλοῖον ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς εἰς ἣν ὑπῆγον.
records.gloss: They were wanting then to take him into the boat, and immediately came to be the boat at the land to which they were going.

L.21: So they wanted to take Him into the boat, and at once the boat came to be at the land toward which they were heading.

R.21: Now they were eager to let Him into the boat. Right away, the boat was at the other side of the lake, where they had been going.

decisions.choice: they wanted to take him in: their fear turned to welcome; John does not say whether he came aboard before they landed
alternatives: they took him into the boat
decisions.reason: The verb means "they wanted" or "they were willing". Mark 6:51 says that Jesus got into the boat. John says only that they wanted to take him in, and then at once they were at land. He may mean that Jesus got in, or that before they could take him in the boat had already arrived.

decisions.choice: immediately at land: part of the wonder, with a possible echo of Psalm 107
alternatives: a natural arrival after more rowing
decisions.reason: "Immediately" makes the arrival sudden, part of what Jesus does, not the end of a long row. Psalm 107:29-30 says of the LORD that he stilled the storm and "brought them to their desired haven". The echo is possible, not certain.

decisions.choice: the other side of the lake, where they had been going
alternatives: the land to which they were going
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly that "the land" was the shore they were making for (Capernaum, verse 17).

records.greek: Τῇ ἐπαύριον ὁ ὄχλος ὁ ἑστηκὼς πέραν τῆς θαλάσσης εἶδον ὅτι πλοιάριον ἄλλο οὐκ ἦν ἐκεῖ εἰ μὴ ἕν, καὶ ὅτι οὐ συνεισῆλθεν τοῖς μαθηταῖς αὐτοῦ ὁ Ἰησοῦς εἰς τὸ πλοῖον ἀλλὰ μόνοι οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ ἀπῆλθον·
records.gloss: On the next day the crowd, the [one] having stood on the other side of the sea, saw that boat other not was there except one, and that not went in with the disciples of him the Jesus into the boat, but alone the disciples of him went away;

L.22: On the next day the crowd that was standing on the other side of the sea saw that no other small boat had been there except one, and that Jesus had not gone into the boat with His disciples, but His disciples had gone away alone.

R.22: The next day the crowd was still on the other side of the lake. They knew that only one boat had been there. They also knew that Jesus had not gotten into it with His disciples. The disciples had left without Him.

decisions.choice: a long sentence that sets the scene; the story picks it up again in 6:24
decisions.reason: John piles up what the crowd had noticed: only one boat had been there the evening before, and Jesus had not gone off in it with his disciples (6:16-17). The sentence then breaks off; 6:23 adds a remark about other boats, and 6:24 starts again with "so when the crowd saw". The point of it all is the crowd's puzzle: Jesus had not left by boat, yet he was gone. They know nothing of his walking on the sea (6:19-21).

decisions.choice: the other side of the sea: the shore where the crowd had been fed
decisions.reason: The crowd stayed on the far side of the Sea of Galilee from Capernaum, where Jesus had fed them (6:1-13). The same phrase in 6:25 means the opposite shore, around Capernaum: John speaks from wherever the crowd is not.

decisions.choice: except one (SBLGNT)
alternatives: except that one into which his disciples had got (many later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: The earliest manuscripts end the clause with "one". Many later ones add words saying which boat this was, the one the disciples had taken; the addition explains the sentence but does not change its sense. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:his|His}}, {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}
decisions.reason: Every pronoun for Christ or for God uses the deity_pronoun setting, including "me" and "my" when Jesus speaks of himself and "you" when people speak to him. At the start of a sentence "He" or "My" is written plain. This applies throughout the passage.

decisions.choice: two sentences (B); five short sentences (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek sentence is tangled (meaning decision m1). Balanced and Readable break it where the thought allows; Literal keeps it whole. Readable says "without him" for "alone", which is what "alone" means here.

decisions.choice: lake
decisions.reason: The Sea of Galilee is a freshwater lake; Readable uses the plain word so a young reader does not picture the ocean. 6:25 does the same.

records.heading: The bread of life

records.greek: ἀλλὰ ἦλθεν πλοιάρια ἐκ Τιβεριάδος ἐγγὺς τοῦ τόπου ὅπου ἔφαγον τὸν ἄρτον εὐχαριστήσαντος τοῦ κυρίου.
records.gloss: But came boats from Tiberias near the place where they ate the bread, having given thanks the Lord.

L.23: But small boats came from Tiberias near the place where they ate the bread after the Lord had given thanks.

R.23: But some boats from the town of Tiberias came to shore near the place where the people had eaten the bread after the Lord gave thanks for it.

decisions.choice: after the Lord had given thanks (SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: Nearly all manuscripts have the phrase. A few witnesses leave it out, among them Codex Bezae and some early Latin and Syriac versions. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the Lord: the narrator's name for Jesus, recalling the meal
decisions.reason: John's narrative rarely calls Jesus "the Lord" before the resurrection (also 4:1 and 11:2); after it, the disciples do so often (20:20; 21:7, 12). Here the thanksgiving of 6:11 is singled out as the mark of that meal: the bread was eaten after he gave thanks.

decisions.choice: Tiberias: the new city on the west shore
decisions.reason: Herod Antipas founded Tiberias on the west shore of the lake about AD 20 and named it after the emperor Tiberius. John has already called the lake "the Sea of Tiberias" (6:1; also 21:1). Boats from there give the crowd a way across.

decisions.choice: but: boats did come, though Jesus had not left by boat
decisions.reason: The oldest manuscripts are written without accents, so the same letters can be read as "but" or as "other" ("other boats came"). The SBLGNT reads "but", setting these boats against the single boat of 6:22. Either way the sense is the same: there were now boats for the crowd.

decisions.choice: had eaten (B, R); the people (R)
decisions.reason: English needs the earlier past for a meal that happened the day before. Readable names who ate, since "they" could be taken as the people on the boats.

decisions.choice: the town of Tiberias; came to shore; for it
decisions.reason: Readable says that Tiberias was a town, that the boats landed, and what the thanks were for (6:11).

records.greek: ὅτε οὖν εἶδεν ὁ ὄχλος ὅτι Ἰησοῦς οὐκ ἔστιν ἐκεῖ οὐδὲ οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ, ἐνέβησαν αὐτοὶ εἰς τὰ πλοιάρια καὶ ἦλθον εἰς Καφαρναοὺμ ζητοῦντες τὸν Ἰησοῦν.
records.gloss: When therefore saw the crowd that Jesus not is there nor the disciples of him, got in they into the boats and came to Capernaum seeking the Jesus.

L.24: So when the crowd saw that Jesus was not there, nor His disciples, they themselves got into the boats and came to Capernaum, seeking Jesus.

R.24: The crowd saw that Jesus was not there, and that His disciples were not there either. So they got into those boats and went across to Capernaum to look for Him.

decisions.choice: so when: the story picks up from 6:22
decisions.reason: The word translated "so" takes up the thread that 6:22 left hanging, after the remark about the boats in 6:23. The crowd has waited and searched, and now gives up on the shore where they ate.

decisions.choice: Capernaum: where Jesus had made his home
decisions.reason: Jesus had stayed in Capernaum with his mother, brothers and disciples (2:12), and his disciples had set out for it the evening before (6:17). It was the obvious place to look. 6:59 says the following talk took place in the synagogue there.

decisions.choice: seeking Jesus: the word Jesus takes up in his reply
decisions.reason: John says the crowd came "seeking" Jesus, and Jesus answers by asking why they seek him (6:26). In John, seeking can be true or false: the first disciples are asked "What are you seeking?" (1:38), and some seek Jesus to kill him (7:1).

decisions.choice: neither Jesus nor his disciples were there
alternatives: Jesus was not there, nor his disciples (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced joins the two names in one phrase, as English does; Literal keeps the Greek order, which adds the disciples as an afterthought.

decisions.choice: to look for {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}
decisions.reason: "Seeking" is less common in speech; "look for" is the everyday word. Balanced and Readable say "him", since Jesus was named just before.

records.greek: Καὶ εὑρόντες αὐτὸν πέραν τῆς θαλάσσης εἶπον αὐτῷ· Ῥαββί, πότε ὧδε γέγονας;
records.gloss: And having found him on the other side of the sea they said to him, "Rabbi, when here have you come?"

L.25: And having found Him on the other side of the sea, they said to Him, "Rabbi, when did You come here?"

R.25: They found Jesus on the other side of the lake and asked Him, "Rabbi, when did You get here?"

decisions.choice: when did you come here: they ask about the time, wondering how he crossed
decisions.reason: The question is "when", but behind it is the puzzle of 6:22: there had been no boat for him. The perfect tense asks how long he has been here. Jesus does not answer it; he turns to why they are looking for him (6:26). The crowd knows nothing of what happened on the sea in the night (6:19-21).

decisions.choice: Rabbi: the respectful title for a teacher
decisions.reason: The day before, this crowd called Jesus "the prophet" and wanted to make him king (6:14-15). Now they address him with the ordinary title for a teacher, which John explained at 1:38.

decisions.choice: the other side of the sea: the Capernaum shore
decisions.reason: Seen from where they had been fed, Capernaum is on the other side (see the note at 6:22).

decisions.choice: Rabbi
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice for John: John translates the word himself (1:38), so every level keeps it.

decisions.choice: get here
decisions.reason: The everyday way of asking about someone's arrival.

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθη αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰησοῦς καὶ εἶπεν· Ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, ζητεῖτέ με οὐχ ὅτι εἴδετε σημεῖα ἀλλ’ ὅτι ἐφάγετε ἐκ τῶν ἄρτων καὶ ἐχορτάσθητε·
records.gloss: Answered them the Jesus and said, "Truly truly I say to you, you seek me not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled;

L.26: Jesus answered them and said, "Truly, truly I say to you, you are seeking Me not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled.

R.26: Jesus answered, "I tell you the truth: you are not looking for Me because you saw what the signs meant. You are looking for Me because you ate the bread and were full.

decisions.choice: saw signs: saw what the signs pointed to
decisions.reason: The crowd had watched the feeding and even called it a sign (6:14). Jesus says they did not see signs: they saw a meal, not what it pointed to, who he is and what he gives. In John a sign is meant to lead to believing (2:11; 20:30-31). The plural takes in the healings that drew the crowd in the first place (6:2).

decisions.choice: were filled: had full stomachs
decisions.reason: ἐχορτάσθητε is a plain word for eating until one is full; it was first used of feeding animals. It is the word of 6:12 ("when they were filled"). Jesus sets their full stomachs against the signs they missed.

decisions.choice: you are seeking me: an ongoing search
decisions.reason: The present tense describes what they have been doing since the morning (6:22-24). The same verb ends 6:24.

decisions.choice: Truly, truly I say to you (L); Truly, truly, I tell you (B); I tell you the truth (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide rendering for John (see 1:51), recorded once in this passage; it covers 6:32 as well.

decisions.choice: ate your fill (B); saw what the signs meant ... were full (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced uses an everyday phrase for being filled. Readable spells out what "seeing signs" means here (meaning decision m1) and repeats "you are looking for me" to keep the two reasons apart.

records.greek: ἐργάζεσθε μὴ τὴν βρῶσιν τὴν ἀπολλυμένην ἀλλὰ τὴν βρῶσιν τὴν μένουσαν εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον, ἣν ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ὑμῖν δώσει, τοῦτον γὰρ ὁ πατὴρ ἐσφράγισεν ὁ θεός.
records.gloss: Work not [for] the food the perishing, but [for] the food the remaining to life eternal, which the Son of the Man to you will give; this one for the Father sealed, the God.

L.27: Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that remains to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you; for the Father, God, has sealed Him."

R.27: Do not work hard for food that goes bad. Work for the food that lasts and gives eternal life, the life of the age to come, which starts now. The Son of Man will give you this food, because God the Father has put His seal on Him. That seal shows that He comes from God."

decisions.choice: food that perishes, food that remains: what passes away against what lasts
decisions.reason: ἀπόλλυμι is the word of 6:12, "so that nothing is lost", and of 6:39, "that I should lose none". μένουσαν is John's word "remain", which he later uses of the bond between Jesus and those who eat his bread (6:56; 15:4). The manna itself went bad if it was kept overnight (Exodus 16:20).

decisions.choice: working for food that does not satisfy
decisions.reason: The thought is close to Isaiah 55:2, which asks why people spend their money and their labor on what is not bread and cannot satisfy. There too God invites people to come and eat what gives life (Isaiah 55:1-3). Jesus is not telling them to stop earning a living but to set their hearts on the food that lasts, which in the end is a gift ("which the Son of Man will give").

decisions.choice: set his seal: marked him as his own and confirmed him
alternatives: the seal is a particular event, such as the Spirit coming down on Jesus at his baptism (1:32-33)
decisions.reason: A seal pressed into wax marked who owned something and vouched that it was genuine. God has confirmed the Son as his own and given him authority. 3:33-34 uses the same picture: whoever accepts his testimony puts a seal to it that God is true. The sentence ends with "God", placed last for weight: the Father who did this is God himself.

decisions.choice: the Son of Man will give: a gift still to come
decisions.reason: Jesus uses his title for himself (1:51; 3:13-14). The future tense looks ahead to 6:51: "the bread that I will give is my flesh, for the life of the world".

decisions.choice: passes away ... remains (B); goes bad ... lasts (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps "remains", John's recurring word (see docs/john-terms.md), and uses an everyday word for perishing. Readable uses the plainest words for food that spoils and food that does not.

decisions.choice: the life of the age to come, which starts now; That seal shows that he comes from God
decisions.reason: Readable explains "eternal life" once in this passage, and says what the seal means (meaning decision m3). It turns "for" into "because" so the link between the gift and the seal is plain.

records.greek: εἶπον οὖν πρὸς αὐτόν· Τί ποιῶμεν ἵνα ἐργαζώμεθα τὰ ἔργα τοῦ θεοῦ;
records.gloss: They said therefore to him, "What may we do, so that we may work the works of the God?"

L.28: So they said to Him, "What should we do, so that we may work the works of God?"

R.28: They asked Jesus, "What should we do? What kind of work does God want from us?"

decisions.choice: the works of God: the deeds God requires and approves
decisions.reason: The genitive can mean either. The crowd asks what they must do, so they mean the works God asks of people, such as keeping his commandments.

decisions.choice: they take up Jesus's word "work" and think of deeds to perform
decisions.reason: Jesus told them to work for the food that remains (6:27). They hear it as a call to do more good deeds, and ask for a list. Jesus answers with one work, not many (6:29).

decisions.choice: the works that God asks of us (B); What kind of work does God want from us? (R)
decisions.reason: "Work the works" is not English. Balanced and Readable state the sense the crowd means (meaning decision m1); Readable splits the question in two.

decisions.choice: asked
decisions.reason: What they say is a question.

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθη ὁ Ἰησοῦς καὶ εἶπεν αὐτοῖς· Τοῦτό ἐστιν τὸ ἔργον τοῦ θεοῦ ἵνα πιστεύητε εἰς ὃν ἀπέστειλεν ἐκεῖνος.
records.gloss: Answered the Jesus and said to them, "This is the work of the God, that you believe in whom sent that one."

L.29: Jesus answered and said to them, "This is the work of God, that you believe in [the one] whom He sent."

R.29: Jesus answered, "The work God wants from you is this: believe in the one He sent."

decisions.choice: the work of God: the work God asks of you
alternatives: the work God does in you
decisions.reason: As an answer to 6:28, the phrase means what God requires. Yet the wording also allows the other sense, and the chapter goes on to say that no one can come to Jesus unless the Father draws him (6:44, 65): the believing God asks for is also his own work. The choice follows the question; the footnote gives the other side.

decisions.choice: one work, not many
decisions.reason: They asked about "works", plural (6:28); Jesus answers with a single "work". What God asks is not a list of deeds but believing.

decisions.choice: believe in the one he sent: keep trusting the one God sent
decisions.reason: The present tense describes an ongoing believing, and "believe in" (with εἰς) means to put one's trust in a person. ἐκεῖνος ("that one") is God, and the one he sent is Jesus himself, who speaks of himself in the third person, as in 5:38.

decisions.choice: The work God wants from you
decisions.reason: Readable states the sense chosen in meaning decision m1. Literal and Balanced keep the phrase, which can carry both senses.

records.greek: εἶπον οὖν αὐτῷ· Τί οὖν ποιεῖς σὺ σημεῖον, ἵνα ἴδωμεν καὶ πιστεύσωμέν σοι;
records.gloss: They said therefore to him, "What then do you do [as] sign, so that we may see and may believe you?

L.30: So they said to Him, "What sign then do You do, so that we may see and believe You?

R.30: So they asked Him, "Then what sign will You show us? If we see it, we will believe You.

decisions.choice: they ask for a sign, the day after the feeding
decisions.reason: They had eaten the bread the day before and called it a sign (6:14). Now they want more, and 6:31 shows what they have in mind: Moses gave bread from heaven for forty years in the wilderness, not one meal. The demand for a sign is the same as in 2:18 (compare 4:48).

decisions.choice: you: emphatic, you as against Moses
decisions.reason: The pronoun σὺ is written out, which makes it emphatic. The contrast with Moses comes in the next sentence.

decisions.choice: believe you: believe what you say
decisions.reason: With a plain dative, "believe" means to accept a person's word as true. Jesus spoke of believing "in" the one God sent (6:29); the crowd offers only to believe his claim if he proves it.

decisions.choice: perform (B); show us (R)
decisions.reason: "Do a sign" is not natural English. Readable turns the purpose clause into a promise, "If we see it, we will believe you", which is what the crowd means.

records.greek: τί ἐργάζῃ;
records.gloss: What do you work?"

decisions.choice: they turn Jesus's word back on him
decisions.reason: Jesus told them to work (6:27) and spoke of the work of God (6:29). Now they ask what work he himself does. The verb is the one Jesus used in 5:17: "My Father has been at work right up to now, and I am at work as well."

decisions.choice: What work ... do
decisions.reason: English cannot say "what do you work"; every level uses the noun "work" to keep the echo of 6:27-29. Readable's "can" brings out the challenge in the question.

records.greek: οἱ πατέρες ἡμῶν τὸ μάννα ἔφαγον ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ, καθώς ἐστιν γεγραμμένον· Ἄρτον ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ἔδωκεν αὐτοῖς φαγεῖν.
records.gloss: The fathers of us the manna ate in the wilderness, as it is written, 'Bread from the heaven he gave them to eat.'"

L.31: Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, as it is written, 'Bread from heaven He gave them to eat.'"

R.31: Our ancestors ate manna in the desert. The Scriptures say, 'He gave them bread from heaven to eat.'"

decisions.choice: the manna passages: Psalm 78:24; Exodus 16:4, 15; Nehemiah 9:15
decisions.reason: The words are not an exact quotation of any one verse. Psalm 78:24 says God rained down manna for them to eat and gave them the grain of heaven; in Exodus 16:4 God says, "I will rain bread from heaven for you", and in 16:15 Moses tells the people that the manna is bread the LORD has given them; Nehemiah 9:15 recalls it in prayer. The whole of Jesus's answer in 6:32-58 works through this one sentence: who gave, what the bread from heaven is, and what eating it means.

decisions.choice: he gave: God, in Scripture; the crowd may be thinking of Moses
decisions.reason: In every passage quoted it is God who gives the manna. But Jesus answers "it is not Moses who has given you the bread from heaven" (6:32), so the crowd seems to credit Moses, or to hold up Moses as the prophet a new sign must match.

decisions.choice: the hope of manna again
decisions.reason: Moses promised that God would raise up a prophet like him (Deuteronomy 18:15), and the crowd had just called Jesus "the prophet" (6:14). A Jewish writing from about the end of the first century, 2 Baruch 29:8, says that when the Messiah comes the store of manna will come down from on high again. Feeding a crowd once falls short, in their eyes, of Moses's forty years.

decisions.choice: ancestors
decisions.reason: "Fathers" here means forebears; "ancestors" says so plainly, as at 4:20.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} (L); He (B, R)
decisions.reason: The giver in the Scripture quoted is God (meaning decision m2), so the pronoun takes the deity_pronoun setting in Literal, which keeps the Greek order; in Balanced and Readable it begins the quotation and is capitalised either way. Readable says "desert" for wilderness and "The Scriptures say" for "it is written".

records.greek: εἶπεν οὖν αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, οὐ Μωϋσῆς δέδωκεν ὑμῖν τὸν ἄρτον ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, ἀλλ’ ὁ πατήρ μου δίδωσιν ὑμῖν τὸν ἄρτον ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ τὸν ἀληθινόν·
records.gloss: Said therefore to them the Jesus, "Truly truly I say to you, not Moses has given you the bread from the heaven, but the Father of me gives you the bread from the heaven the true;

L.32: So Jesus said to them, "Truly, truly I say to you, it is not Moses [who] has given you the bread from heaven, but My Father gives you the bread from heaven, the true [one].

R.32: Jesus said to them, "I tell you the truth: Moses was not the one who gave you bread from heaven. It is My Father who gives you the true bread from heaven.

decisions.choice: not Moses: the giver of the manna was God
decisions.reason: The word "not" stands first, against "Moses". Moses himself told Israel that the manna was bread given by the LORD (Exodus 16:15). Jesus corrects the crowd's reading of the verse they quoted (6:31).

decisions.choice: has given ... gives: the old gift and the gift being given now
decisions.reason: The first verb is a perfect, looking back at the manna; the second is a present: the Father is giving the true bread now, to "you", the people standing before Jesus. He is the one who calls God "my Father" (5:17-18).

decisions.choice: true: real, the reality the manna pointed to
decisions.reason: ἀληθινόν means genuine, the real thing, as with the true light (1:9) and the true vine (15:1). The manna was real food, but it was a sign of the bread that gives life to the world (6:33). The Greek puts "the true" last, for weight.

decisions.choice: Moses was not the one who gave ... my Father is the one who gives (B, R)
alternatives: not Moses has given ... but my Father gives (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable keep the contrast between the two givers by naming each one first, in the same pattern. Balanced puts "true" before "bread" as English does; Literal keeps it at the end.

records.greek: ὁ γὰρ ἄρτος τοῦ θεοῦ ἐστιν ὁ καταβαίνων ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ καὶ ζωὴν διδοὺς τῷ κόσμῳ.
records.gloss: The for bread of the God is the [one] coming down from the heaven and life giving to the world."

L.33: For the bread of God is the [one] coming down from heaven and giving life to the world."

R.33: God's bread is the bread that comes down from heaven and gives life to the world."

decisions.choice: the bread that comes down
decisions.reason: The Greek participle can refer back to "bread" (that which comes down) or stand for a person (he who comes down). The crowd takes it as bread, since they ask for some (6:34), and the sentence describes what kind of bread God gives. Only in 6:35 does Jesus say "I am the bread", and in 6:38 "I have come down from heaven"; the wording here prepares for that without yet saying it.

decisions.choice: comes down from heaven: like the manna, and like the Son
decisions.reason: The manna came down on the camp with the dew (Numbers 11:9). The same verb is used of the Son of Man, who came down from heaven (3:13), and Jesus will say it of himself in 6:38, 41, 50-51.

decisions.choice: the world: humanity, not one nation
decisions.reason: The manna fed Israel in the wilderness; this bread gives life to the world, all people, as in 3:16 and 4:42 ("the Savior of the world").

decisions.choice: the bread that
decisions.reason: Readable repeats "bread" so the reader follows the sense chosen in meaning decision m1. Literal keeps "[the one]" and Balanced "the one that", which say no more than the Greek.

records.greek: εἶπον οὖν πρὸς αὐτόν· Κύριε, πάντοτε δὸς ἡμῖν τὸν ἄρτον τοῦτον.
records.gloss: They said therefore to him, "Sir, always give us the bread this."

L.34: So they said to Him, "Sir, always give us this bread."

R.34: So they said to Him, "Sir, please give us this bread every day from now on!"

decisions.choice: Sir: a respectful address
alternatives: Lord, a confession of who Jesus is
decisions.reason: Κύριε is the polite form used to anyone of standing. The crowd does not yet know who Jesus is; within a few sentences they grumble at him (6:41). A footnote gives "Lord".

decisions.choice: they ask for bread as the Samaritan woman asked for water
decisions.reason: The request is almost the same as hers: "Sir, give me this water!" (4:15). Like her, they think of a gift that would meet ordinary needs for good, as the manna came every day (Exodus 16:4, 35).

decisions.choice: Sir
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice for those who do not yet know who Jesus is (meaning decision m1; see docs/john-terms.md).

decisions.choice: all the time (B); every day from now on (R)
decisions.reason: "Always" here means without stopping, like the daily manna. Readable adds "please" for the tone of a request.

records.greek: Εἶπεν αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἄρτος τῆς ζωῆς· ὁ ἐρχόμενος πρὸς ἐμὲ οὐ μὴ πεινάσῃ, καὶ ὁ πιστεύων εἰς ἐμὲ οὐ μὴ διψήσει πώποτε.
records.gloss: Said to them the Jesus, "I am the bread of the life; the [one] coming to me not not will hunger, and the [one] believing in me not not will thirst ever.

L.35: Jesus said to them, "I am the bread of life; the one coming to Me will certainly not hunger, and the one believing in Me will certainly never thirst.

R.35: Jesus told them, "I am the bread that gives life. People who come to Me will never be hungry. People who believe in Me will never be thirsty, not ever.

decisions.choice: I am the bread of life: the first of John's sayings "I am" with a picture
decisions.reason: With a predicate, "I am" is ordinary grammar (see 4:26 and 8:58 for the use without one). This is the first of seven such sayings in John: the bread of life, the light of the world (8:12), the door (10:7, 9), the good shepherd (10:11), the resurrection and the life (11:25), the way, the truth and the life (14:6), and the true vine (15:1). The "I" is written out and emphatic: the bread they asked for (6:34) is not a thing but a person.

decisions.choice: the bread of life: the bread that gives life
decisions.reason: The genitive describes what the bread does, as 6:33 has just said: it gives life to the world. 6:51 calls it "the living bread".

decisions.choice: coming and believing are one act; the double negative is emphatic
decisions.reason: The two halves say the same thing in two ways, as Hebrew poetry does: to come to Jesus is to believe in him. οὐ μή is the strongest way of saying "not", and πώποτε ("ever") adds more weight to the second half.

decisions.choice: never hunger or thirst: God's promises in Isaiah
decisions.reason: Isaiah promises God's people that "they shall not hunger or thirst" (Isaiah 49:10), and calls the thirsty and the hungry to come and eat and live (Isaiah 55:1-3). Jesus told the Samaritan woman that whoever drinks the water he gives will never thirst (4:14).

decisions.choice: the bread that gives life
decisions.reason: Readable states the sense of the phrase (meaning decision m2). Literal and Balanced keep the familiar wording, which is the plain translation.

decisions.choice: certainly not ... certainly never (L); never ... never at any time (B); never ... never ... not ever (R)
decisions.reason: Each level marks the emphatic negative (meaning decision m3) in its own register, and keeps the extra "ever" of the second half.

records.greek: ἀλλ’ εἶπον ὑμῖν ὅτι καὶ ἑωράκατέ με καὶ οὐ πιστεύετε.
records.gloss: But I said to you that both you have seen me and not you believe.

L.36: But I told you that you have both seen Me and do not believe.

R.36: But I told you before. You have seen Me with your own eyes, and you do not believe.

decisions.choice: I told you: Jesus refers to what he has already said in substance
alternatives: a saying not recorded in the Gospel
decisions.reason: No earlier verse has these exact words. The nearest are 6:26, that they saw and did not see the signs, and 5:38-40, "you do not believe the one he sent"; it is also possible that Jesus refers to words John does not record.

decisions.choice: you have seen me (SBLGNT)
alternatives: you have seen, and do not believe (some early witnesses)
decisions.reason: Most manuscripts have "me". Some early witnesses leave it out, among them Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Alexandrinus and some Latin and Syriac versions; the sense would then be "you have seen [the signs]". Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: seeing without believing
decisions.reason: The crowd asked for a sign "so that we may see and believe" (6:30). Jesus says they have seen more than a sign, they have seen him, and still do not believe. Compare 20:29, where Jesus calls blessed those who believe without having seen.

decisions.choice: with your own eyes
decisions.reason: Readable stresses that they have really seen him, which is the force of "both ... and" (meaning decision m3).

records.greek: πᾶν ὃ δίδωσίν μοι ὁ πατὴρ πρὸς ἐμὲ ἥξει, καὶ τὸν ἐρχόμενον πρός με οὐ μὴ ἐκβάλω ἔξω, ὅτι καταβέβηκα ἀπὸ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ οὐχ ἵνα ποιῶ τὸ θέλημα τὸ ἐμὸν ἀλλὰ τὸ θέλημα τοῦ πέμψαντός με·
records.gloss: All that gives to me the Father to me will come, and the [one] coming to me not not I will cast outside, \v 38 because I have come down from the heaven not that I may do the will the mine but the will of the [one] having sent me;

L.37: Everything that the Father gives Me will come to Me, and the one coming to Me I will by no means cast outside,
L.38: because I have come down from heaven not so that I may do the will that is Mine, but the will of the one who sent Me.

R.37: Everyone the Father gives to Me will come to Me. And I will never turn away anyone who comes to Me.
R.38: That is because I came down from heaven, not to do what I want, but to do what the one who sent Me wants.

decisions.choice: everything that: the people given to Jesus, seen as one whole
decisions.reason: πᾶν ὃ is neuter, "everything that": John speaks of all whom the Father gives as one gift, then of each person ("the one who comes"). He does the same in 6:39 and 17:2.

decisions.choice: the Father's giving and a person's coming
decisions.reason: Those the Father gives will come; Jesus will not turn away anyone who comes. The first half says that coming to Jesus rests on the Father's gift (6:44, 65; 17:6); the second, that no one who comes will be refused. The text holds both without explaining how they fit.

decisions.choice: I will never cast out: I will welcome and keep
decisions.reason: The emphatic "by no means" (οὐ μή) with "cast outside" says, by denying the opposite, that he will receive and hold on to everyone who comes. 6:39 says the same positively. Compare the man who is cast out of the synagogue, whom Jesus then seeks out (9:34-35).

decisions.choice: he came down to do the will of the one who sent him
decisions.reason: Jesus now says of himself what he said of the bread: it comes down from heaven (6:33). He gives his reason for welcoming all who come: he is not acting on his own will but on the Father's, which 6:39-40 spell out. Compare 4:34 and 5:30.

decisions.choice: Everyone
decisions.reason: In English "everything" sounds like things, not people. Balanced and Readable say "everyone", which is already inclusive; Literal keeps the neuter (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: never send away (B); never turn away (R)
decisions.reason: Plain words for refusing someone who comes asking (meaning decision m3). Readable says "what I want" and "what the one who sent me wants" for "will".

records.greek: τοῦτο δέ ἐστιν τὸ θέλημα τοῦ πέμψαντός με ἵνα πᾶν ὃ δέδωκέν μοι μὴ ἀπολέσω ἐξ αὐτοῦ ἀλλὰ ἀναστήσω αὐτὸ τῇ ἐσχάτῃ ἡμέρᾳ.
records.gloss: This and is the will of the [one] having sent me, that all that he has given me not I may lose of it, but I may raise up it on the last day.

L.39: And this is the will of the one who sent Me, that all that He has given Me, I should not lose [any] of it, but should raise it up on the last day.

R.39: The one who sent Me wants this: I must not lose any of the people He has given Me. Instead, I will raise them all from the dead on the last day.

decisions.choice: all that he has given me ... it: the whole people given, as in 6:37
decisions.reason: The neuter "all that" is picked up by "it" twice: not one part of the Father's gift will be lost, and all of it will be raised.

decisions.choice: lose: let perish
decisions.reason: ἀπολέσω is the verb of the leftover pieces in 6:12 ("so that nothing is lost") and of the food that perishes in 6:27; with people it means to perish, as in 3:16. What Jesus did with the bread, he does with those given to him.

decisions.choice: raise up on the last day: the bodily resurrection at the end
decisions.reason: The "last day" is the day of resurrection and judgment (11:24; 12:48). The phrase comes four times in this chapter (6:39, 40, 44, 54). John holds together life that starts now (6:40, 47) and raising at the end, as in 5:24-29.

decisions.choice: it all
decisions.reason: Balanced adds "all" so "it" clearly means the whole of what was given (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: them ... raise them all from the dead
decisions.reason: Readable names the people meant by "it" and says what raising means here (meaning decision m3). The same wording is used for the refrain in 6:40.

records.greek: τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν τὸ θέλημα τοῦ πατρός μου ἵνα πᾶς ὁ θεωρῶν τὸν υἱὸν καὶ πιστεύων εἰς αὐτὸν ἔχῃ ζωὴν αἰώνιον, καὶ ἀναστήσω αὐτὸν ἐγὼ τῇ ἐσχάτῃ ἡμέρᾳ.
records.gloss: This for is the will of the Father of me, that everyone the [one] looking on the Son and believing in him may have life eternal, and will raise up him I on the last day."

L.40: For this is the will of My Father, that everyone who looks on the Son and believes in Him should have eternal life, and I Myself will raise them up on the last day."

R.40: My Father wants everyone who sees the Son and believes in Him to have eternal life. And I Myself will raise them from the dead on the last day."

decisions.choice: looks on the Son: sees him with attention, and so comes to believe
decisions.reason: θεωρῶν means to look at something with attention. It is not the seeing of 6:36, where the crowd saw and did not believe; here looking and believing go together. In 3:14-15 Jesus compared himself to the bronze serpent, which the bitten Israelites looked at and lived (Numbers 21:8-9).

decisions.choice: has eternal life now, and will be raised on the last day
decisions.reason: The will of the Father is that the one who believes should have eternal life, a present possession (5:24), and that Jesus should raise that person on the last day. The two are not alternatives: life starts now and is completed at the resurrection.

decisions.choice: I myself will raise
decisions.reason: The pronoun ἐγὼ is written out, which makes it emphatic: Jesus himself will raise the dead, the work 5:21 and 5:25-29 give to the Son.

decisions.choice: {{gender:them|him}}
decisions.reason: "Him" refers to "everyone who looks on the Son", men and women alike, so it takes the gender setting. "Him" in "believes in him" is the Son and takes the deity_pronoun setting.

decisions.choice: sees
decisions.reason: The everyday word. Readable turns "this is the will of my Father, that" into "My Father wants", as in 6:39, and says "from the dead" for the raising.

records.greek: Ἐγόγγυζον οὖν οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι περὶ αὐτοῦ ὅτι εἶπεν· Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἄρτος ὁ καταβὰς ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, καὶ ἔλεγον· Οὐχ οὗτός ἐστιν Ἰησοῦς ὁ υἱὸς Ἰωσήφ, οὗ ἡμεῖς οἴδαμεν τὸν πατέρα καὶ τὴν μητέρα;
records.gloss: Were grumbling therefore the Jews about him because he said, "I am the bread the [one] having come down out of the heaven," \v 42 and they were saying, "Not this is Jesus the son of Joseph, of whom we know the father and the mother?

L.41: So the Jews were grumbling about Him because He said, "I am the bread that came down out of heaven,"
L.42: and they were saying, "Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we ourselves know?

R.41: Then the Jewish people there began to grumble about Jesus, because He had said, "I am the bread that came down from heaven."
R.42: They said, "This is Jesus, Joseph's son! We know His father and mother.

decisions.choice: the Jews: the crowd in the synagogue at Capernaum, people of Galilee, not the authorities from Jerusalem
decisions.reason: The scene is the synagogue in Capernaum (6:59), and the speakers are the crowd that had eaten the loaves and crossed the lake to look for Jesus (6:22-25). What they say shows they are local people: they know Joseph, and Jesus's mother (verse 42). Nothing in the passage says that authorities had come from Jerusalem, as they do in 1:19 and Mark 7:1, though leaders of the local synagogue may be among them. John stops calling them "the crowd" and calls them "the Jews" at the point where they begin to reject what Jesus says. The word marks their response, not a difference of people: Jesus and his disciples are Jews too (4:9, 4:22).

decisions.choice: grumbling: the word for Israel's grumbling in the wilderness
alternatives: ordinary complaining, with no echo of Scripture
decisions.reason: The talk has been about the manna (6:31-32), and the verb Ἐγόγγυζον is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for Israel grumbling against Moses and against God over food in the wilderness, the very complaint that God answered by sending manna (Exodus 16:2-12; Numbers 11:1-6; 14:27). The crowd repeats what their ancestors did, and Jesus will say "your fathers ate the manna ... and died" (6:49). The tense pictures a muttering that went on among them (verse 43; compare 7:12 and 7:32), not one open protest.

decisions.choice: they judge his origin by the family they know
decisions.reason: The crowd reasons that a man whose parents they know cannot have come down from heaven. John lets the reader see the irony: they know where he comes from in one sense (7:27-28) but not in the sense that matters (8:14), for he is the Word who became flesh (1:14). Philip had already called him "son of Joseph" (1:45). The pronoun ἡμεῖς is stated, so it is emphatic: we, of all people, know his family. The passage does not say whether Joseph was still alive.

decisions.choice: the Jewish people there
decisions.reason: Readable names the group plainly, as the John term list asks: here the people of the synagogue in Capernaum (meaning decision m1). It does not say "leaders", because nothing in the scene points to the authorities.

decisions.choice: Surely this is Jesus ...? (B); This is Jesus ...! (R)
decisions.reason: The question begins with a negative that expects the answer yes. Balanced and Readable make that plain; Literal keeps the form of the question.

records.greek: πῶς νῦν λέγει ὅτι Ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ καταβέβηκα;
records.gloss: How now does he say, "Out of the heaven I have come down"?"

L.42: How is it that He now says, 'Out of heaven I have come down'?"

R.42: So how can He claim, 'I came down from heaven'?"

decisions.choice: now: after all this, in the face of what we know
alternatives: now, at this moment, as opposed to earlier
decisions.reason: νῦν here has the force of "in these circumstances": given that they know his family, how can he say such a thing? It is an objection, not a question about the time when he began to say it.

decisions.choice: they quote his own words from 6:38
decisions.reason: The word ὅτι introduces a direct quotation, and the words that follow repeat what Jesus said in 6:38, with the same perfect tense: he came down and is now here. They have heard him exactly; their problem is not that they misheard but that they will not accept it.

decisions.choice: what does he mean by saying
decisions.reason: "How" here challenges the claim rather than asks for an explanation (meaning decision m1). Balanced puts it as a challenge in natural English; Readable uses "how can he claim".

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθη Ἰησοῦς καὶ εἶπεν αὐτοῖς· Μὴ γογγύζετε μετ’ ἀλλήλων.
records.gloss: Answered Jesus and said to them, "Not grumble with one another.

L.43: Jesus answered and said to them, "Do not grumble with one another.

R.43: Jesus told them, "Stop grumbling to each other.

decisions.choice: stop grumbling: the present command tells them to end what they are already doing
decisions.reason: γογγύζετε is a present command with a negative, which commonly forbids something already going on (compare 2:16 and 5:14). Their grumbling had begun in verse 41.

decisions.choice: with one another: talk among themselves, not words addressed to him
decisions.reason: The grumbling was among the crowd (verse 41 says it was "about him"). Jesus answers it all the same; John has already said that Jesus knew what was in people (2:24-25).

decisions.choice: answered and said (L); answered them (B)
decisions.reason: "Answered and said" is a common Greek way of introducing a reply; the second verb adds no separate action. Literal keeps both verbs, Balanced and Readable use one.

records.greek: οὐδεὶς δύναται ἐλθεῖν πρός με ἐὰν μὴ ὁ πατὴρ ὁ πέμψας με ἑλκύσῃ αὐτόν, κἀγὼ ἀναστήσω αὐτὸν ἐν τῇ ἐσχάτῃ ἡμέρᾳ.
records.gloss: No one is able to come to me if not the Father the [one] having sent me draws him, and I will raise up him in the last day.

L.44: No one is able to come to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws them, and I will raise them up on the last day.
