R.44: No one can come to Me unless the Father, who sent Me, draws them to Me. And on the last day I will raise them from the dead.

decisions.choice: draws: the Father's own work that brings a person to Jesus
alternatives: only invites or attracts, leaving the rest to the person
decisions.reason: The verb ἑλκύσῃ is used of hauling a net (21:6, 21:11) and drawing a sword (18:10), so it is a strong word: the coming starts with the Father, not with the person. But in Scripture God draws people with love (Jeremiah 31:3, where the Greek Old Testament uses this verb), and Jesus says that when he is lifted up he will draw all people to himself (12:32). The next verse says how the drawing happens: people hear the Father and learn from him (6:45). The sentence does not say whether the drawing can be refused.

decisions.choice: God's initiative and human believing are both affirmed
decisions.reason: Jesus says here, as in 6:37 and 6:65, that coming to him depends on the Father. In the same chapter he calls people to believe and promises life to everyone who does (6:29, 6:35, 6:40, 6:47). The passage holds both together and does not explain how they fit; Christians have answered that question in different ways.

decisions.choice: the raising on the last day: bodily resurrection at the end of the age
decisions.reason: This is the third of four times the promise is made in this chapter (6:39, 6:40, 6:44, 6:54). The last day is the day of resurrection, as Martha understands it (11:24; compare 5:28-29). The one who believes already has eternal life (6:47); the raising on the last day completes it.

decisions.choice: {{gender:them|him}}
decisions.reason: "Him" stands for anyone at all who comes, man or woman, so the gender setting applies (as at 3:2).

decisions.choice: draws them to me; raise them from the dead
alternatives: draws them; raise them up (Literal, Balanced)
decisions.reason: Readable says where the Father draws people, to Jesus, which the start of the sentence implies, and what "raise up" means here (meaning decision m3).

records.greek: ἔστιν γεγραμμένον ἐν τοῖς προφήταις· Καὶ ἔσονται πάντες διδακτοὶ θεοῦ· πᾶς ὁ ἀκούσας παρὰ τοῦ πατρὸς καὶ μαθὼν ἔρχεται πρὸς ἐμέ.
records.gloss: It is having been written in the prophets, "And they will be all taught of God." Everyone the [one] having heard from the Father and having learned comes to me.

L.45: It is written in the Prophets, 'And they will all be taught by God.' Everyone who has heard from the Father and has learned comes to Me.

R.45: The Prophets wrote, 'God will teach all of them.' Everyone who hears what the Father says and learns from it comes to Me.

decisions.choice: Isaiah 54:13: all will be taught by God
decisions.reason: The words come from Isaiah 54:13, a promise to restored Jerusalem that all her children will be taught by the Lord. The Hebrew has the divine name there; the Greek translation of Isaiah has "God", and so does John. Jeremiah 31:33-34 makes the same promise for the new covenant, when all will know the Lord. Isaiah says "your children"; Jesus's "all" leaves out the limit.

decisions.choice: the Prophets: a section of Scripture
alternatives: a group of people, the prophets
decisions.reason: Jews of the time spoke of the Scriptures as the Law and the Prophets (Luke 24:44; Acts 13:15). "In the Prophets" names the part of Scripture where the words stand, the way 1:45 speaks of what Moses wrote "in the Law".

decisions.choice: the Father draws people by teaching them
decisions.reason: This sentence explains the drawing of 6:44. Those whom God teaches, who have heard from the Father and learned, come to Jesus. Coming to Jesus is the sign that someone has heard the Father; refusing him shows the opposite (5:37-38; 8:47).

decisions.choice: taught by God
decisions.reason: The Greek has "God", so every level keeps it, though the Hebrew of Isaiah has the divine name (meaning decision m1). "Of God" in the gloss is the Greek form; "by God" is the English sense. Readable says "God will teach".

decisions.choice: the Prophets, with a capital
decisions.reason: A capital shows that this names a part of Scripture (meaning decision m2), not the prophets as people.

records.greek: οὐχ ὅτι τὸν πατέρα ἑώρακέν τις εἰ μὴ ὁ ὢν παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ, οὗτος ἑώρακεν τὸν πατέρα.
records.gloss: Not that the Father has seen anyone, if not the [one] being from the God, this [one] has seen the Father.

L.46: Not that anyone has seen the Father, except the one who is from God: this one has seen the Father.

R.46: I do not mean that anyone has seen the Father. The only one who has seen the Father is the one who comes from God.

decisions.choice: not that: a correction, so verse 45 is not misread
decisions.reason: οὐχ ὅτι heads off a wrong conclusion. Hearing and learning from the Father (6:45) does not mean that anyone sees the Father directly. People hear the Father through the one he has sent.

decisions.choice: the one from God is Jesus himself, the only one who has seen the Father
decisions.reason: Jesus speaks of himself in the third person, as he often does (3:13; 5:19). The sentence repeats the claim of 1:18: no one has ever seen God, and the only Son has made him known. Compare 3:11, 3:32 and 7:29, "I know him, because I am from him".

decisions.choice: from God: coming from God's own presence
alternatives: sent by God, as a prophet is sent
decisions.reason: τοῦ with the genitive means "from beside". The same phrase can be used of a messenger such as John the Baptist (1:6). Here, though, the one who is from God is the one who has seen the Father, so it means coming from God's presence, as in 16:27-28 and 17:8.

decisions.choice: has come from God (B); comes from God (R)
decisions.reason: "Is from God" can sound like a statement about birthplace or about character; "has come from" makes the movement plain, as in 16:28.

records.greek: ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, ὁ πιστεύων ἔχει ζωὴν αἰώνιον.
records.gloss: Truly truly I say to you, the [one] believing has life eternal.

L.47: Truly, truly I say to you, the one who believes has eternal life.

R.47: I tell you the truth: anyone who believes has eternal life already.

decisions.choice: the one who believes, with no object (SBLGNT)
alternatives: the one who believes in me (many later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add "in me" after "believes". The earliest papyri and the major early manuscripts do not have it, and the SBLGNT follows them; the addition looks like a natural way of filling out the sense. The meaning is the same either way, since the whole passage is about believing in Jesus (6:29, 6:35, 6:40). A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: has: eternal life is held now
alternatives: will have, only in the future
decisions.reason: The verb is present. Eternal life begins when a person believes (3:36; 5:24), and the raising on the last day (6:44) completes it.

decisions.choice: Truly, truly I say to you (L); Truly, truly, I tell you (B); I tell you the truth (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide rendering for John (see 1:51), recorded once in this passage; it covers 6:53 as well.

decisions.choice: already
decisions.reason: Readable makes plain that the present tense means now (meaning decision m2).

records.greek: ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἄρτος τῆς ζωῆς·
records.gloss: I am the bread of the life;

L.48: I am the bread of life.

R.48: I am the bread that gives life.

decisions.choice: bread of life: the bread that gives life
decisions.reason: The bread is described by what it does: it gives life to the world (6:33) and those who eat it will not die (6:50). In 6:51 Jesus also calls it "living bread". The saying repeats 6:35 and begins the comparison with the manna in the next sentences.

decisions.choice: I am, with a predicate: an ordinary statement, the first of John's images
alternatives: an echo of the divine name
decisions.reason: Here "I am" is followed by what he is, so it is an ordinary statement of identity, as in 8:12 (the light of the world) and 10:11 (the good shepherd). The uses without a predicate, which echo God's name, come later (8:24, 8:58).

decisions.choice: the bread that gives life
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what "of life" means (meaning decision m1).

records.greek: οἱ πατέρες ὑμῶν ἔφαγον ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ τὸ μάννα καὶ ἀπέθανον·
records.gloss: The fathers of you ate in the wilderness the manna and died;

L.49: Your fathers ate in the wilderness the manna, and they died.

R.49: Your ancestors ate manna in the wilderness, but they still died.

decisions.choice: the manna: the food God gave Israel in the wilderness
decisions.reason: God gave the manna each morning for forty years (Exodus 16; Numbers 11:7-9). The crowd had quoted Psalm 78:24, "he gave them bread from heaven to eat" (6:31). That generation died in the wilderness (Numbers 14:29-35).

decisions.choice: fathers: ancestors, men and women
decisions.reason: πατέρες is the usual word for forebears, as in 4:20. The crowd had said "our fathers" (6:31); Jesus answers "your fathers", taking up their own claim. He is not setting himself apart from Israel.

decisions.choice: died: bodily death, which the manna could not prevent
decisions.reason: The manna kept people alive for a day at a time but did not stop them dying. That is the contrast with the bread from heaven that Jesus is, which gives life that does not end (verses 50-51).

decisions.choice: Your {{gender:ancestors|fathers}}
decisions.reason: The word means the people of that generation, men and women (meaning decision m2), so the gender setting applies. Literal keeps "fathers", the form of the Greek.

records.greek: οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ ἄρτος ὁ ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ καταβαίνων ἵνα τις ἐξ αὐτοῦ φάγῃ καὶ μὴ ἀποθάνῃ·
records.gloss: This is the bread the [one] out of the heaven coming down, so that anyone of it may eat and not die;

L.50: This is the bread that comes down out of heaven, so that anyone may eat of it and not die.

R.50: But this bread comes down from heaven. Anyone who eats it will not die.

decisions.choice: this: the bread that Jesus is, coming down from heaven
decisions.reason: "This" points back to Jesus's words "I am the bread of life" (6:48). Set beside verse 49, it marks a contrast with the manna. The present participle speaks of the bread as coming down, what it is and does (compare 6:33).

decisions.choice: not die: not lose life in the full sense, though the body dies
decisions.reason: Those who eat the manna died (verse 49), and believers die too. Jesus's promise is that death does not end the life he gives: "even if they die, they will live" (11:25-26), and he will raise them on the last day (6:54).

decisions.choice: Here, by contrast (B); But (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek sets this sentence directly beside verse 49 with no linking word. Balanced and Readable add a word to show the contrast between the manna and this bread (meaning decision m1).

records.greek: ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἄρτος ὁ ζῶν ὁ ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ καταβάς· ἐάν τις φάγῃ ἐκ τούτου τοῦ ἄρτου ζήσει εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα, καὶ ὁ ἄρτος δὲ ὃν ἐγὼ δώσω ἡ σάρξ μού ἐστιν ὑπὲρ τῆς τοῦ κόσμου ζωῆς.
records.gloss: I am the bread the living the [one] out of the heaven having come down; if anyone eats of this the bread he will live into the age, and the bread also which I will give the flesh of me is, for the of the world life.

L.51: I am the living bread that came down out of heaven; if anyone eats of this bread, they will live forever; and the bread that I will give is My flesh, for the life of the world."

R.51: I am the bread that is alive, the bread that came down from heaven. Anyone who eats this bread will live forever. The bread I will give is My flesh. I give it for the world, so that the world can have life."

decisions.choice: living: alive and giving life
decisions.reason: ζῶν means alive. As with the "living water" of 4:10, the bread is not only alive itself but gives life to those who receive it (6:57).

decisions.choice: flesh: his human body and life, given up in death
alternatives: body, as in the words at the Last Supper
decisions.reason: σάρξ recalls 1:14, "the Word became flesh": the bread is the human life of the Son of God. The future "I will give" looks ahead to his death. The other Gospels' account of the Last Supper uses a different word, "body" (Mark 14:22), and John keeps his own word all through this passage (6:51-56).

decisions.choice: for: on behalf of, for the sake of the world's life
decisions.reason: In John ὑπὲρ with the genitive is used again and again of Jesus's death for others: the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (10:11, 10:15), one man dies for the people (11:50-52; 18:14), a man lays down his life for his friends (15:13). Here the gift of his flesh is for the life of the world, the people God loved and sent his Son to save (3:16-17).

decisions.choice: the bread that I will give is my flesh, for the life of the world (SBLGNT)
alternatives: the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world (many later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts repeat "which I will give" before "for the life of the world", which smooths the sentence. The earliest manuscripts have the shorter text, which the SBLGNT follows. The meaning does not change. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: will live forever
decisions.reason: "Into the age" is a Greek idiom for "forever"; English has no such phrase, so even Literal says "forever".

decisions.choice: and I give it so that the world may have life (B); I give it for the world, so that the world can have life (R)
alternatives: for the life of the world (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable spell out the compressed phrase as a clause (meaning decision m3), so that "for" is not read as "in exchange for". Every level keeps "flesh" rather than "body" (meaning decision m2).

records.greek: Ἐμάχοντο οὖν πρὸς ἀλλήλους οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι λέγοντες· Πῶς δύναται οὗτος ἡμῖν δοῦναι τὴν σάρκα αὐτοῦ φαγεῖν;
records.gloss: Were fighting therefore with one another the Jews, saying, "How is able this [one] to us to give the flesh of him to eat?"

L.52: So the Jews were fighting with one another, saying, "How is this [man] able to give us His flesh to eat?"

R.52: Then the Jewish people there started arguing with each other. "This man wants to give us His flesh to eat?" they said. "How could He do that?"

decisions.choice: the Jews: the same crowd as in 6:41, the people in the synagogue at Capernaum
decisions.reason: The group is the one that grumbled in verse 41, in the same place (6:59). Nothing shows that the authorities are in view; see the note at 6:41.

decisions.choice: were fighting: a sharp dispute, worse than the grumbling
decisions.reason: Ἐμάχοντο means to fight or quarrel; here it is a fight with words. The muttering of verse 41 has become an open quarrel. "With one another" suggests they did not all agree, as the crowds are divided over Jesus in 7:43, 9:16 and 10:19.

decisions.choice: they take his words in the most physical sense, and Jesus does not soften them
decisions.reason: As Nicodemus did with being born again (3:4) and the Samaritan woman with living water (4:11), the hearers take Jesus's words at the most physical level. Here Jesus does not explain the saying away; he repeats it more strongly (6:53-56). What the words do mean is taken up at 6:53 and 6:63.

decisions.choice: the Jewish people there
decisions.reason: As at 6:41, Readable names the group plainly (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: he (B); This man (R)
decisions.reason: "This one" can sound dismissive in Greek. Balanced uses a simple pronoun; Readable keeps "this man" and splits the question in two to keep it short.

records.greek: εἶπεν οὖν αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, ἐὰν μὴ φάγητε τὴν σάρκα τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου καὶ πίητε αὐτοῦ τὸ αἷμα, οὐκ ἔχετε ζωὴν ἐν ἑαυτοῖς.
records.gloss: Said therefore to them the Jesus, "Truly truly I say to you, if not you eat the flesh of the Son of the Man and drink of him the blood, not you have life in yourselves.

L.53: So Jesus said to them, "Truly, truly I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink His blood, you do not have life in yourselves.

R.53: Jesus told them, "I tell you the truth: you must eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink His blood. If you do not, you have no life in you.

decisions.choice: eating his flesh and drinking his blood: what the words say, and the main ways they have been read
decisions.reason: Jesus restates his saying more starkly, adding the blood. The words have been read in two main ways, which are often held together. Some read them as speaking of the Lord's Supper, where believers eat the bread and drink the cup that Jesus gave as his body and blood (Mark 14:22-24; 1 Corinthians 10:16; 11:23-26). Others read them as a vivid picture of believing in Jesus and receiving the life he gives through his death, since the same promises are made to the one who believes (6:35, 6:40, 6:47) and Jesus later says that his words are spirit and life (6:63). The text does not settle the question between these readings, and the translation gives the words as they stand.

decisions.choice: drinking blood was forbidden in the Law, so the saying would shock
decisions.reason: God's law forbade eating meat with the blood in it, because the life is in the blood (Genesis 9:4; Leviticus 17:10-14; compare Acts 15:20). To hear of drinking anyone's blood would have been deeply offensive to Jewish listeners, which helps explain the reaction of many disciples in 6:60-66. Flesh and blood named separately also suggest a death in which the blood is shed.

decisions.choice: life in yourselves: life of your own, coming from him
decisions.reason: The phrase recalls 5:26: the Father has life in himself and has given the Son to have life in himself. Without receiving the Son, people have no such life in them. "Life" here is the eternal life of 6:54.

decisions.choice: if you do not ... there is no life in you (B); you must ... If you do not, you have no life in you (R)
alternatives: unless you ... you do not have life in yourselves (Literal)
decisions.reason: Readable turns the condition into a plain command followed by its consequence, to keep the sentences short. Both levels say "in you" for "in yourselves", which sounds natural and means the same.

records.greek: ὁ τρώγων μου τὴν σάρκα καὶ πίνων μου τὸ αἷμα ἔχει ζωὴν αἰώνιον, κἀγὼ ἀναστήσω αὐτὸν τῇ ἐσχάτῃ ἡμέρᾳ.
records.gloss: The [one] chewing of me the flesh and drinking of me the blood has life eternal, and I will raise up him in the last day.

L.54: The one who feeds on My flesh and drinks My blood has eternal life, and I will raise them up on the last day.

R.54: Those who eat My flesh and drink My blood have eternal life. On the last day I will raise them from the dead.

decisions.choice: eats: a change of verb that most likely means no more than "eat"
alternatives: chew or munch, stressing physical eating
decisions.reason: Up to verse 53 the word for eating is the one used in φάγῃ and φάγητε. From here on (6:54, 6:56, 6:57, 6:58) it is τρώγων. In older Greek this verb meant to munch or chew, and some read the change as stressing real eating. But in New Testament times it was often simply "eat" (Matthew 24:38), and John never uses the present tense of the other verb: every present-tense "eat" in his Gospel is this one, including 13:18, where Jesus quotes Psalm 41:10, "the one who eats my bread". Here all four uses are present participles, so the change most likely comes from the tense.

decisions.choice: the same promises as for believing in 6:40
decisions.reason: This verse matches 6:40 almost clause for clause. There everyone who looks to the Son and believes in him has eternal life and will be raised on the last day; here it is the one who eats his flesh and drinks his blood. Some take the parallel to show that eating and drinking are a picture of believing; others take it to mean that believing is expressed in sharing the Lord's Supper. See the note at 6:53.

decisions.choice: eats and drinks: present tense, an ongoing feeding
decisions.reason: In 6:50-53 the verbs were aorist, looking at eating as a whole. Here the present participles describe the one who keeps feeding on him, as "the one who believes" (6:47) describes a person who goes on believing.

decisions.choice: feeds on (L); eats (B, R)
decisions.reason: Literal uses a different English verb wherever the Greek changes verb (6:54-58), so readers can see the change; "chews" would overstate it (meaning decision m1). Balanced and Readable say "eat", as the verb most likely means.

decisions.choice: raise them from the dead
decisions.reason: As at 6:44, Readable says what the raising is. It uses the plural "those who", which needs no gender setting.

records.greek: ἡ γὰρ σάρξ μου ἀληθής ἐστι βρῶσις, καὶ τὸ αἷμά μου ἀληθής ἐστι πόσις.
records.gloss: The for flesh of me true is food, and the blood of me true is drink.

L.55: For My flesh is food that is true, and My blood is drink that is true.

R.55: My flesh is food in the fullest sense, and My blood is drink in the fullest sense.

decisions.choice: true (an adjective) twice (SBLGNT)
alternatives: truly (an adverb): my flesh truly is food, and my blood truly is drink (some manuscripts)
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT reads ἀληθής, "true", following early manuscripts. Other manuscripts, including many later ones, read ἀληθῶς, "truly": "my flesh truly is food". The difference is small: one says what kind of food it is, the other insists that it really is food. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: true: genuine food, that does what food is for
decisions.reason: The word means real or genuine. The manna fed people only for a time, and they died (6:49); the food Jesus gives lasts and gives eternal life (6:27). It is food that fully does what food is meant to do. The sentence does not by itself say how the eating takes place; see the note at 6:53.

decisions.choice: for: the reason for verse 54
decisions.reason: The sentence explains why the one who eats and drinks has eternal life: because this is the real food and drink.

decisions.choice: genuine (B); in the fullest sense (R)
decisions.reason: "True food" can sound as if other food were false. Balanced uses "genuine", and Readable explains the sense (meaning decision m2).

records.greek: ὁ τρώγων μου τὴν σάρκα καὶ πίνων μου τὸ αἷμα ἐν ἐμοὶ μένει κἀγὼ ἐν αὐτῷ.
records.gloss: The [one] chewing of me the flesh and drinking of me the blood in me remains and I in him.

L.56: The one who feeds on My flesh and drinks My blood remains in Me, and I in them.

R.56: Those who eat My flesh and drink My blood remain in Me, and I remain in them.

decisions.choice: remains: a lasting, living union
decisions.reason: μένει is a favorite word of John, used for staying in a place (1:38-39) and for a lasting union with Jesus. This is the first time in the Gospel that it describes the bond between Jesus and those who are his. The theme returns in the image of the vine (15:4-10) and in 1 John 3:24 and 4:13-16.

decisions.choice: a mutual indwelling: they in him and he in them
decisions.reason: The result of eating and drinking here is that the person remains in Jesus and Jesus in them. The same two-way union is described elsewhere in terms of keeping his words and his love (15:4-10; 1 John 3:24), and it mirrors the union of the Father and the Son (14:10-11, 14:20; 17:21-23). On the main lines of reading the eating and drinking, see the note at 6:53.

decisions.choice: the sentence ends here (SBLGNT)
alternatives: a longer text in one manuscript, continuing with words about the Father and the Son and about receiving the body of the Son of Man
decisions.reason: One early manuscript, Codex Bezae, adds a further sentence at this point. No other early manuscript has it, and the SBLGNT does not. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: and I remain in them
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable repeat the verb, which the Greek leaves understood. Literal has the shorter form. The gender setting applies where the singular "him" means anyone; Readable's plural needs none.

records.greek: καθὼς ἀπέστειλέν με ὁ ζῶν πατὴρ κἀγὼ ζῶ διὰ τὸν πατέρα, καὶ ὁ τρώγων με κἀκεῖνος ζήσει δι’ ἐμέ.
records.gloss: Just as sent me the living Father and I live because of the Father, also the [one] chewing me, that [one] also will live because of me.

L.57: Just as the living Father sent Me, and I live because of the Father, so also the one who feeds on Me, that one also will live because of Me.

R.57: The Father who sent Me is alive, and I have life from Him. In the same way, anyone who feeds on Me will have life from Me.

decisions.choice: the living Father: God, who has life in himself
decisions.reason: Only here does Jesus say "the living Father". It echoes the Old Testament's "living God" (Deuteronomy 5:26; Psalm 42:3; Hosea 1:10), the God who has life in himself and gives it (5:26). Life passes from the Father to the Son, and from the Son to those who feed on him.

decisions.choice: because of: the Father is the source of the Son's life, and the Son of the believer's
alternatives: for the sake of: I live for the Father, and they will live for me
decisions.reason: διὰ with the accusative usually gives the cause or ground: the Son lives because of the Father, and the one who feeds on him will live because of him. Some take it as the goal (living for the sake of), but the chain of life in this sentence and in 5:26 points to the source.

decisions.choice: feeds on me: what is received is Jesus himself
decisions.reason: Here the object is no longer "my flesh" but "me". Whatever the eating means, what is received is the person of Jesus, the living one. This does not by itself settle how the earlier verses should be read; see the note at 6:53.

decisions.choice: feeds on me
decisions.reason: With a person as its object, "eats" sounds strange in English, so every level says "feeds on" here. Readable says "have life from" for "live because of" (meaning decision m2).

records.greek: οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ ἄρτος ὁ ἐξ οὐρανοῦ καταβάς, οὐ καθὼς ἔφαγον οἱ πατέρες καὶ ἀπέθανον· ὁ τρώγων τοῦτον τὸν ἄρτον ζήσει εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα.
records.gloss: This is the bread the [one] out of heaven having come down, not as ate the fathers and died; the [one] chewing this the bread will live into the age.

L.58: This is the bread that came down out of heaven, not as the fathers ate and died; the one who feeds on this bread will live forever."

R.58: So this is the bread that came down from heaven. It is not like the manna the ancestors ate. They died, but anyone who eats this bread will live forever."

decisions.choice: the fathers ate (SBLGNT)
alternatives: your fathers ate the manna (many later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts read "your fathers ate the manna", filling out the phrase from 6:31 and 6:49. The earliest manuscripts have the shorter text, which the SBLGNT follows. The meaning is the same. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: not as the fathers ate: unlike the bread the fathers ate, who died anyway
decisions.reason: The comparison is compressed: the bread from heaven is not like what the ancestors ate in the wilderness, for they ate and still died (6:49).

decisions.choice: the summary of the teaching that began at 6:31
decisions.reason: The sentence draws together the whole discussion: the crowd's words about bread from heaven (6:31), Jesus's claim to be that bread (6:35, 6:41, 6:48-51), the contrast with the manna (6:49-50), and the promise of life forever (6:51). "This bread" and "my flesh" are one subject: the verb for eating used with his flesh (6:54-57) is now used with the bread.

decisions.choice: the food the {{gender:ancestors|fathers}} ate (B); the manna the {{gender:ancestors|fathers}} ate (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable supply what the ancestors ate, since English cannot leave it out; Readable names the manna, as in 6:49. The gender setting applies as at 6:49. Literal says "feeds on" here, as at 6:54.

records.greek: ταῦτα εἶπεν ἐν συναγωγῇ διδάσκων ἐν Καφαρναούμ.
records.gloss: These things he said in synagogue teaching in Capernaum.

L.59: These things He said in [the] synagogue, teaching in Capernaum.

R.59: Jesus said all this while He was teaching in the synagogue, the Jewish meeting house in Capernaum.

decisions.choice: in synagogue: in the synagogue, during a gathering
alternatives: in an assembly (the meeting rather than the building)
decisions.reason: συναγωγῇ has no article, as is common in set phrases about places (compare 18:20). It can mean the building or the gathering held in it. Capernaum had a synagogue, where Jesus taught on the Sabbath (Mark 1:21; Luke 7:5), and the phrase most likely means that one.

decisions.choice: the synagogue: the place where Jews gathered to hear Scripture read and taught
decisions.reason: Jews met in the synagogue on the Sabbath to read and explain the Law and the Prophets, and a visiting teacher could be invited to speak (Luke 4:16-21; Acts 13:15). This explains why Jesus quotes and explains Scripture (6:31, 6:45).

decisions.choice: these things: the teaching from 6:26 onward
decisions.reason: The note of place closes the whole discussion with the crowd that found Jesus in Capernaum (6:24-25). It also shows that the hearers of 6:41 and 6:52 were people of the synagogue there.

decisions.choice: [the] synagogue (L); the synagogue (B, R); the Jewish meeting house (R)
decisions.reason: English needs an article (meaning decision m1). Readable briefly explains the word "synagogue", which some readers may not know (meaning decision m2).

records.greek: Πολλοὶ οὖν ἀκούσαντες ἐκ τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτοῦ εἶπαν· Σκληρός ἐστιν ὁ λόγος οὗτος· τίς δύναται αὐτοῦ ἀκούειν;
records.gloss: Many therefore having heard of the disciples of him said, "Hard is the word this; who is able it to hear?"

L.60: So many of His disciples, when they heard [this], said, "This word is hard; who is able to listen to it?"

R.60: Many of Jesus's disciples heard this and said, "These words are too hard to take. Who can keep listening to them?"

decisions.choice: his disciples: the wider circle of people who followed Jesus, not only the Twelve
decisions.reason: John uses "disciples" of everyone who had attached themselves to Jesus as their teacher. The Twelve are named as a separate, smaller group a few verses later (6:67), after many of these disciples have left (6:66). Those who object here are followers, not the crowd of 6:41 and 6:52.

decisions.choice: hard: harsh and offensive, hard to accept
decisions.reason: The word describes something rough or severe, not something obscure. The disciples' difficulty is not that they cannot follow Jesus's meaning but that they cannot stomach it: he has just said that unless they eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood they have no life in them (6:53-58).

decisions.choice: listen to it: hear the word with acceptance
decisions.reason: The pronoun αὐτοῦ can refer either to "this word" or to Jesus, since both are masculine in Greek. The word is the nearer and more natural reference, and the sense is the same either way. To "hear" here means to listen and accept, as in 8:43 and 8:47 and of the sheep who hear the shepherd's voice (10:3, 27).

decisions.choice: message ... bear to listen (B); these words ... keep listening (R)
decisions.reason: "Word" here means what Jesus has been saying in 6:35-58, so Balanced says "message" and Readable "these words". "Bear to listen" and "keep listening" show that the problem is accepting what was said (meaning decisions m2, m3).

records.heading: Many disciples turn back

records.greek: εἰδὼς δὲ ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἐν ἑαυτῷ ὅτι γογγύζουσιν περὶ τούτου οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ εἶπεν αὐτοῖς· Τοῦτο ὑμᾶς σκανδαλίζει;
records.gloss: Knowing but the Jesus in himself that are grumbling about this the disciples of him, said to them, "This you causes to stumble?

L.61: But Jesus, knowing in Himself that His disciples were grumbling about this, said to them, "Does this cause you to stumble?

R.61: Jesus knew without being told that His disciples were complaining about this. So He said to them, "Is this making you stumble and fall away?

decisions.choice: knowing in himself: Jesus knew without being told
decisions.reason: The phrase stresses that Jesus knew their reaction from within himself. John often notes that Jesus knew what was in people (1:47-48; 2:24-25; 4:17-18), and the narrator says the same again in 6:64.

decisions.choice: grumbling: the same word used of the crowd in 6:41 and 6:43
decisions.reason: Now the disciples do what the crowd did. The word recalls Israel grumbling in the wilderness, where God gave them manna (Exodus 16:2-12; Numbers 11:1-6), the story behind this whole chapter (6:31, 49, 58).

decisions.choice: cause to stumble: to trip someone up so that they fall away
alternatives: offend, in the sense of annoy or insult
decisions.reason: The verb pictures a stumbling block that makes someone fall. In John it means losing hold of faith: in 16:1 Jesus tells his disciples he has warned them "so that you will not fall away" with the same verb. That is what happens in 6:66.

decisions.choice: stumble
decisions.reason: "Offend" in current English means to hurt someone's feelings, which is too weak. "Stumble" keeps the picture of tripping and falling (meaning decision m3).

decisions.choice: without being told (R); and fall away (R)
decisions.reason: Readable spells out what "in himself" (meaning decision m1) and "stumble" (meaning decision m3) mean here.

records.greek: ἐὰν οὖν θεωρῆτε τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἀναβαίνοντα ὅπου ἦν τὸ πρότερον;
records.gloss: If then you see the Son of the man going up where he was the before?

L.62: [What] then if you see the Son of Man going up [to] where He was before?

R.62: What will you think, then, if you see the Son of Man going back up to the place where He was before?

decisions.choice: an unfinished "if": the sentence breaks off and leaves the conclusion unsaid
alternatives: what if you see ... ? Then you would stumble even more
what if you see ... ? Then you would no longer stumble
decisions.reason: The Greek has the "if" half of a sentence and no "then" half. Jesus leaves his hearers to finish it. It may mean that seeing him go up would be an even greater shock, or that it would show his words to be true and remove the stumbling block. John leaves both open, and so does this translation, as an open question.

decisions.choice: going up to where he was before: returning to the Father, from whom he came
decisions.reason: All through the chapter Jesus is the bread that came down from heaven (6:33, 38, 41, 50-51, 58). Now he speaks of going back up. No one has gone up into heaven except the one who came down from it, the Son of Man (3:13); compare 1:51 and 20:17. In John his going up passes through the cross, where the Son of Man is "lifted up" (3:14; 12:32-34).

decisions.choice: [What] then if (L); Then what if (B); What will you think, then, if (R)
decisions.reason: English needs a word to show that the "if" clause is a question with its answer left unsaid (meaning decision m1). Readable asks the question outright without answering it.

records.greek: τὸ πνεῦμά ἐστιν τὸ ζῳοποιοῦν, ἡ σὰρξ οὐκ ὠφελεῖ οὐδέν· τὰ ῥήματα ἃ ἐγὼ λελάληκα ὑμῖν πνεῦμά ἐστιν καὶ ζωή ἐστιν.
records.gloss: The Spirit is the [one] giving life, the flesh not profits nothing; the words which I have spoken to you spirit is and life is.

L.63: The Spirit is the one giving life; the flesh profits nothing. The words which I have spoken to you are spirit and are life.

R.63: God's Spirit is the one who gives life. Human nature on its own can do nothing to help. The words I have spoken to you come from the Spirit, and they give life.

decisions.choice: the Spirit: the Spirit of God, who gives life
alternatives: the spiritual side of a person, as against the body
decisions.reason: "Spirit" and "flesh" stand against each other here as they do in 3:6: what is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit. The one who gives new life is God's Spirit (3:5-8), whom Jesus will give after he is glorified (7:39). The verb "gives life" is used of the Father and the Son in 5:21.

decisions.choice: the flesh: human nature on its own, apart from the Spirit
alternatives: Jesus's own flesh, as if he were taking back 6:51-58
decisions.reason: Jesus says "the flesh", not "my flesh". He is not cancelling what he has just said about giving his flesh for the life of the world (6:51). He means that human nature by itself, and a merely physical way of hearing his words, cannot give life, as in 3:6 and 8:15.

decisions.choice: spirit and life: the words belong to the Spirit and bring life
alternatives: the Holy Spirit, as a name
spiritual in the sense of symbolic, not real
decisions.reason: The words are those Jesus has just spoken in this discourse (the perfect tense: "have spoken"). To say they "are spirit" describes what kind of words they are: they come from the Spirit and carry the Spirit's life-giving work. God gives the Spirit without measure to the one whose words he speaks (3:34). The word here is taken as a description of the words, not as a name for the Spirit as a person; the other view takes it as the Holy Spirit himself, given through Jesus's words.

decisions.choice: God's Spirit (R); human nature on its own (R)
decisions.reason: Readable makes plain whose Spirit is meant (meaning decision m1) and what "the flesh" means here (meaning decision m2), since "flesh" in this chapter could otherwise be taken as Jesus's own flesh.

decisions.choice: come from the Spirit, and they give life (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says what "are spirit and are life" means in plain terms (meaning decision m3).

records.greek: ἀλλὰ εἰσὶν ἐξ ὑμῶν τινες οἳ οὐ πιστεύουσιν.
records.gloss: But are of you some who not believe."

L.64: But there are some of you who do not believe."

R.64: But some of you do not believe."

decisions.choice: believe: trust in Jesus as the one the Father sent
decisions.reason: These people are disciples who have followed Jesus (6:60), but following is not yet believing in the sense of this chapter: coming to him and trusting him as the bread of life (6:29, 35, 40, 47). John has already told of people whose believing Jesus did not trust (2:23-25).

decisions.choice: some of you: some of the disciples Jesus is speaking to
decisions.reason: The "you" is the group of disciples who were grumbling (6:61). Jesus does not say all of them; the next verses show that unbelief reaches even into the Twelve (6:70-71).

decisions.choice: Yet some among you do not believe
alternatives: But there are some of you who do not believe (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced drops the "there are ... who" construction for a simpler English sentence with the same meaning.

records.greek: ᾔδει γὰρ ἐξ ἀρχῆς ὁ Ἰησοῦς τίνες εἰσὶν οἱ μὴ πιστεύοντες καὶ τίς ἐστιν ὁ παραδώσων αὐτόν.
records.gloss: Knew for from beginning the Jesus who are the [ones] not believing and who is the [one] going to hand over him.

L.64: For Jesus knew from [the] beginning who the ones not believing were, and who the one was who would hand Him over.

R.64: Jesus had known from the very beginning which of them did not believe. He also knew who was going to betray Him.

decisions.choice: from the beginning: from the start, when these people first came to him
alternatives: from the beginning of all things (1:1)
decisions.reason: Here the phrase means the start of Jesus's work with his disciples, as in 15:27 and 16:4, not the beginning of creation. The narrator explains Jesus's words in 6:64a: he was not taken by surprise. John says the same when the betrayal draws near (13:11, 18-19).

decisions.choice: hand over: give someone up to their enemies, here by betrayal
alternatives: hand over, with no thought of betrayal
decisions.reason: The verb means to hand someone over. John uses it of the Jewish authorities handing Jesus to Pilate (18:30, 35) and of Pilate handing him over to be crucified (19:16). Used of Judas, a friend and one of the Twelve (6:71), it means betrayal. This is the first mention of the betrayer in John; he is named in 6:71.

decisions.choice: the ones not believing: unbelief among those who had been following Jesus
decisions.reason: The same participle as "everyone who believes" (3:15-16; 6:40, 47), with "not". Jesus's knowledge does not cause their unbelief; the next verse says that coming to him is the Father's gift (6:65).

decisions.choice: hand over (L); betray (B, R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the plain sense of the verb so the reader can see that it is the same word used of the authorities and Pilate. Balanced and Readable say "betray", since that is what Judas's handing over was (meaning decision m2).

records.greek: καὶ ἔλεγεν· Διὰ τοῦτο εἴρηκα ὑμῖν ὅτι οὐδεὶς δύναται ἐλθεῖν πρός με ἐὰν μὴ ᾖ δεδομένον αὐτῷ ἐκ τοῦ πατρός.
records.gloss: And he was saying, "Because of this I have said to you that no one is able to come to me unless it is having been given to him from the Father."

L.65: And He was saying, "Because of this I have said to you that no one is able to come to Me unless it has been given to them from the Father."

R.65: Then He said, "That is why I told you that no one can come to Me unless the Father makes it possible for them."

decisions.choice: I have told you: Jesus repeats 6:37 and 6:44
decisions.reason: Earlier in the discourse Jesus said that everyone the Father gives him will come to him (6:37) and that no one can come to him unless the Father who sent him draws them (6:44). Coming to Jesus is believing in him (6:35).

decisions.choice: because of this: because some do not believe (6:64)
decisions.reason: "This" points back to Jesus's words that some of them do not believe. Their unbelief is the reason he had told them that coming to him is the Father's gift.

decisions.choice: unless it has been given him by the Father: coming to Jesus is the Father's gift
decisions.reason: The form of the verb means a gift already given and still in force. Jesus does not explain how the gift relates to human choice; he says both that the Father gives and draws (6:37, 44) and that people are to blame for not coming (5:40).

decisions.choice: added (B); said (R)
decisions.reason: The past continuous form here introduces further words in the same conversation; Balanced shows that by "added".

decisions.choice: unless the Father makes it possible for them (R)
alternatives: unless it has been given to them by the Father
decisions.reason: Readable names the Father as the giver and says plainly what the gift is: the ability to come (meaning decision m3).

decisions.choice: them, under the gender setting
decisions.reason: "No one" means any person, man or woman; the traditional "him" is the alternative.

records.greek: Ἐκ τούτου πολλοὶ ἐκ τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτοῦ ἀπῆλθον εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω καὶ οὐκέτι μετ’ αὐτοῦ περιεπάτουν.
records.gloss: From this many of the disciples of him went away into the [things] behind and no longer with him were walking.

L.66: From this, many of His disciples went away backward and were no longer walking with Him.

R.66: Because of what Jesus said, many of His disciples left Him. From then on they no longer went around with Him.

decisions.choice: from this: both "because of this" and "from this time on"
decisions.reason: The phrase Ἐκ τούτου can give the cause (because of this) or the time (from then on). John uses it again in 19:12, where both senses also fit. Here the two belong together: these disciples left because of what Jesus said, and from that point they no longer followed him.

decisions.choice: went away backward: turned back, gave up following him
decisions.reason: The phrase means going back to where one came from. Those who had come after Jesus now went back to their former lives. The same verb "go away" is picked up in Jesus's question in 6:67 and Peter's answer in 6:68.

decisions.choice: walking with him: going about with Jesus as his followers
decisions.reason: A teacher's disciples traveled with him from place to place and learned from him as they went. The verb is "walk"; the past tense here describes something they had been doing and now stopped.

decisions.choice: From this (L); At this (B); Because of what Jesus said ... From then on (R)
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced use words that hold both the cause and the time (meaning decision m1). Readable states both outright in two short sentences.

decisions.choice: drew back ... going about with him (B); left him ... went around with him (R)
alternatives: went away backward ... walking with him (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the idiom (meaning decision m2) and the picture of walking with Jesus (meaning decision m3) into everyday English.

records.greek: εἶπεν οὖν ὁ Ἰησοῦς τοῖς δώδεκα· Μὴ καὶ ὑμεῖς θέλετε ὑπάγειν;
records.gloss: Said therefore the Jesus to the twelve, "Not also you want to go away?"

L.67: So Jesus said to the Twelve, "You do not also want to go away, do you?"

R.67: So Jesus asked the twelve disciples He had chosen, "You do not want to leave Me too, do you?"

decisions.choice: the Twelve: the inner group of twelve disciples
decisions.reason: This is the first time John mentions the Twelve. He does not tell how they were chosen (Jesus refers to it in 6:70) and does not list them, which suggests his readers already knew of them. They appear again in 20:24. The number recalls the twelve tribes of Israel.

decisions.choice: a question that expects the answer "no"
alternatives: a neutral question: do you want to go away?
decisions.reason: The Greek form of the question looks for a "no" answer. Jesus gives the Twelve the freedom to leave while expecting that they will stay, and Peter answers in that spirit (6:68).

decisions.choice: you also: you too, like the many who have just left
decisions.reason: The pronoun "you" is written out and joined with "also", setting the Twelve beside the disciples who have gone away (6:66).

decisions.choice: Surely you do not ...?
alternatives: Do you want to go away as well?
decisions.reason: Balanced shows that the question expects "no" (meaning decision m2); Literal does it with a tag question ("do you?").

decisions.choice: the twelve disciples he had chosen; leave me
decisions.reason: Readable explains who the Twelve are, using what Jesus himself says in 6:70, and names whom they would be leaving.

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθη αὐτῷ Σίμων Πέτρος· Κύριε, πρὸς τίνα ἀπελευσόμεθα;
records.gloss: Answered him Simon Peter, "Lord, to whom will we go away?

L.68: Simon Peter answered Him, "Lord, to whom shall we go away?

R.68: Simon Peter answered, "Lord, who else is there for us to go to?

decisions.choice: Lord: Peter addresses Jesus as his master
decisions.reason: The word can be a polite "sir" (4:11; 5:7), but here it is spoken by one of the Twelve in a confession of faith, and it carries the full sense of "Lord" (compare 11:27; 13:6; 20:28).

decisions.choice: go away: Peter takes up the word of 6:66-67
decisions.reason: Many disciples "went away" (6:66), and Jesus asked whether the Twelve also wanted to "go away" (6:67, a related verb). Peter answers with the same verb as 6:66: if they went away from Jesus, there is no one else to go to.

decisions.choice: to whom would we go? (B); who else is there for us to go to? (R)
alternatives: to whom shall we go away? (Literal)
decisions.reason: The question means that there is no one else (meaning decision m2). Readable makes that plain with "else".

records.greek: ῥήματα ζωῆς αἰωνίου ἔχεις, καὶ ἡμεῖς πεπιστεύκαμεν καὶ ἐγνώκαμεν ὅτι σὺ εἶ ὁ ἅγιος τοῦ θεοῦ.
records.gloss: Words of life eternal you have, \v 69 and we have believed and have known that you are the holy [one] of the God."

L.68: You have words of eternal life,
L.69: and we ourselves have believed and have known that You are the Holy One of God."

R.69: We have believed, and we know for sure, that You are God's Holy One."

decisions.choice: the Holy One of God (SBLGNT)
alternatives: the Christ, the Son of the living God
the Christ, the Holy One of God
the Christ, the Son of God
decisions.reason: The earliest manuscripts, among them Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, read "the Holy One of God". Later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read "the Christ, the Son of the living God", which matches Peter's confession in Matthew 16:16, and others combine the readings in different ways. The shorter, unusual title is more likely to have been changed into the familiar one than the other way round. A footnote gives the other reading. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the Holy One of God: the one God has set apart as his own and sent
decisions.reason: The title is rare. In the other Gospels an unclean spirit uses it of Jesus (Mark 1:24; Luke 4:34). In John, Jesus is the one "whom the Father set apart and sent into the world" (10:36), and he sets himself apart for his disciples' sake (17:19). Peter confesses that Jesus belongs wholly to God and comes from him.

decisions.choice: we have believed and have come to know: a settled conviction, reached and still held
alternatives: two stages, first believing and then knowing
decisions.reason: Both verbs are in the perfect tense, which describes a past act whose result still stands. Believing and knowing are not two steps in order: in 17:8 John puts knowing before believing. The pronoun "we" is written out and emphatic: we, unlike those who have left.

decisions.choice: words of eternal life: words that give eternal life
decisions.reason: Peter echoes Jesus in 6:63: the words he has spoken are spirit and life. Whoever hears his word and believes has eternal life (5:24). There is no article: Jesus has words of this kind, and no one else does (6:68a).

decisions.choice: words that bring eternal life (B); Your words give eternal life (R)
alternatives: You have the words of eternal life
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what kind of words these are (meaning decision m4).

decisions.choice: have believed and have known (L); have believed, and we know (B); have believed, and we know for sure (R)
alternatives: have come to believe and to know
decisions.reason: The second perfect describes knowledge that Peter and the others now have (meaning decision m3), so Balanced and Readable put it in the present. Literal keeps the form and shows the emphatic "we" with "we ourselves".

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθη αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Οὐκ ἐγὼ ὑμᾶς τοὺς δώδεκα ἐξελεξάμην;
records.gloss: Answered them the Jesus, "Not I you the twelve chose?

L.70: Jesus answered them, "Was it not I who chose you, the Twelve?

R.70: Jesus answered them, "Remember, I chose all twelve of you myself.

decisions.choice: a question that expects "yes", with the emphasis on "I"
decisions.reason: The form of the question expects agreement, and the pronoun "I" is written out for emphasis: Jesus himself chose them. He says the same in 13:18 ("I know whom I have chosen") and 15:16 ("you did not choose me, but I chose you").

decisions.choice: Jesus answers Peter's "we"
decisions.reason: Peter has spoken for all the Twelve (6:69). Jesus answers them all, and qualifies Peter's "we": he chose all twelve, knowing that one of them would betray him (6:64; 13:18).

decisions.choice: Remember, I chose ... (a statement)
decisions.reason: The question expects "yes" (meaning decision m1), so Readable turns it into a statement, which is easier to follow.

records.greek: καὶ ἐξ ὑμῶν εἷς διάβολός ἐστιν.
records.gloss: And of you one a devil is."

L.70: And of you, one is a devil."

R.70: But one of you is a devil."

decisions.choice: a devil: one who acts as the devil's agent
alternatives: a slanderer or accuser, the word's root meaning
decisions.reason: The word means slanderer or accuser and is used as the name of the devil (8:44; 13:2). Here it has no article: Judas is not the devil himself but one who does the devil's work. The devil puts the betrayal into Judas's heart (13:2), and Satan enters him (13:27). Jesus once called Peter "Satan" when he spoke against Jesus's path to the cross (Mark 8:33).

decisions.choice: and: "and yet", setting the betrayal against the choosing
decisions.reason: The word "and" here joins two facts that clash: Jesus chose the Twelve, and one of them is a devil.

decisions.choice: Still (B); But (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable show the contrast with the previous sentence (meaning decision m2).

records.greek: ἔλεγεν δὲ τὸν Ἰούδαν Σίμωνος Ἰσκαριώτου· οὗτος γὰρ ἔμελλεν παραδιδόναι αὐτόν, εἷς ἐκ τῶν δώδεκα.
records.gloss: He was speaking now [of] the Judas of Simon Iscariot; this [one] for was going to hand over him, one of the twelve.

L.71: Now He was speaking of Judas [son] of Simon Iscariot; for this [man] was going to hand Him over, one of the Twelve.

R.71: Jesus was talking about Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot. Judas was one of the twelve disciples, but later he would betray Jesus.

decisions.choice: Iscariot, describing Simon: Judas son of Simon Iscariot (SBLGNT)
alternatives: Judas son of Simon from Kerioth
decisions.reason: In the SBLGNT the name Iscariot agrees in form with Simon, so it belongs to the father as well as the son, as also in 13:26. Many later manuscripts make it agree with Judas instead. A few, among them the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus, have "from Kerioth" in place of Iscariot. A footnote gives the other readings. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: Iscariot: probably "man of Kerioth"
alternatives: from a word for an assassin
decisions.reason: The meaning of the name is not certain. The most likely explanation is that it comes from the Hebrew for "man of Kerioth", a town in the south of Judea (Joshua 15:25), which the reading "from Kerioth" (m1) supports. Other explanations have been offered, and none can be proved.

decisions.choice: was going to hand him over: betray him, though one of the Twelve
decisions.reason: As in 6:64, the verb is "hand over", and for Judas it means betrayal. "Was going to" looks ahead to what would happen (13:2, 21-30; 18:2-5). The words "one of the Twelve", placed at the end, show how shocking it was: the betrayer came from the chosen inner circle, as in 12:4 and Psalm 41:10, quoted at 13:18.

decisions.choice: hand over (L); betray (B, R)
decisions.reason: As in 6:64 (meaning decision m3).

decisions.choice: [son] of Simon (L); son of Simon (B); the son of Simon (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek gives the father's name with no noun; "son" is understood, as in 1:42 and 21:15.

decisions.choice: but later
decisions.reason: Readable shows the contrast between being one of the Twelve and betraying Jesus (meaning decision m3), and says "Jesus" to make clear who would be betrayed.
